AI Construction Engineering Startup Spacial Taps NYU Prof Ravid Shwartz-Ziv
He will advise the 2-year-old company as it refines its 3D code-compliant construction documents technology
By Philip Russo August 28, 2026 12:26 pm
reprintsSpacial, an artificial intelligence-powered engineering platform for residential construction, announced that Ravid Shwartz-Ziv has joined the company as a scientific adviser.
An assistant professor and faculty fellow at New York University’s Center for Data Science, Shwartz-Ziv leads large language model (LLM) research focused on using information theory to explain what neural networks actually learn. He will work closely with Spacial’s research and engineering teams, advise on major technology decisions for the platform, and assist the founders in establishing its research road map.
Spacial’s platform converts two-dimensional architectural drawings into 3D, code-compliant construction documents with built-in design conflict detection, architectural detailing and local code validation. Founded in 2024, the Palo Alto, Calif.-based startup can turn 2D plans into stamped structural and mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) permit sets in days using AI, plus licensed engineer review.
“Before an engineer will stamp what our model produces, we need real confidence in
what it’s learned, not just how well it performs,” Maor Greenberg, co-founder and CEO of Spacial, said in announcing Shwartz-Ziv’s hire. “The construction industry doesn’t have a
shared standard for proving that an AI-generated plan is accurate and code-compliant. Closing that gap is exactly why we brought Ravid on. He brings deep expertise in evaluating AI systems, and that’s exactly the rigor Spacial needs to get structural AI right.”
Shwartz-Ziv has spent several years benchmarking and evaluating AI systems, which is relevant to a problem the construction industry hasn’t solved: There is no shared standard for measuring whether an AI-generated plan is accurate, code-compliant and internallycoordinated.
In addition, Shwartz-Ziv will guide the evolution of Spacial’s core technology, a model trained to understand buildings as systems of physical relationships. The goal of which is to produce permit-ready engineering documents for construction projects, an issue that is closely aligned with Shwartz-Ziv’s research. He earned a doctorate in brain science and computer science from Hebrew University of Jerusalem and has worked as an AI researcher at Meta, according to his LinkedIn profile.
“Permitting is a hard, practical problem, and Spacial is taking a serious technical
approach to it,” Shwartz-Ziv said in a statement. “Confirming that a model has genuinely learned how buildings work as physical systems, not just that it can produce a plan that looks right, is exactly the kind of question my work on information theory and model evaluation was built to answer. I look forward to supporting the team as an adviser.”
In 2025, Spacial secured $10 million in funding by demonstrating its ability to document progress, reduce rework, and compress pay-app cycles, according to the Center for Real Estate and Technology & Innovation (CRETI). The CRETI report found that the underlying pattern is accelerating: Investors want construction intelligence that produces lender-acceptable evidence, not optional workflow enhancements.
Philip Russo can be reached at prusso@commercialobserver.com.

Kevin Warsh Notes Inflation Concerns But Offers No Clues as to Next Fed Decision
The Fed chair said in Jackson Hole that underlying inflation trends have not ‘meaningfully improved’
By Andrew Coen August 28, 2026 11:24 am
reprintsNew Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh did not tip his hand Friday about whether an interest rate hike is on the horizon but did voice concerns about a continued trend of higher inflation.
“I stand here today committed to a discipline, not to a decision,” Warsh said in prepared remarks at the central bank’s annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyo. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do.”
Warsh, who assumed the Fed leadership post in June from Jerome Powell, stressed Friday that the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) remains committed to keeping its 2 percent annual inflation rate as a target. He said that recent personal consumption expenditures and the consumer price index have performed “better than expected,” but also noted that underlying inflation trends have not “meaningfully improved.”
The FOMC maintained its benchmark interest rates at between 3.5 percent and 3.75 percent during Warsh’s first two meetings. Warsh has sought to change the Fed’s long-standing forward-guidance policy often used by markets when interpreting the central bank’s data, a position he re-emphasized Friday.
“We determine the path of short-term interest rates, and market participants will always try to anticipate what we will do next,” Warsh said. “But we should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade.”
The FOMC’s next meeting is scheduled for Sept. 15-16. Markets have priced in about a 50 percent chance of a rate hike based on Investing.com’s latest Fed rate monitor tool.
Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.

Stratford Partners JV Buys San Diego-Area Apartments for $34M
By Greg Cornfield August 27, 2026 5:25 pm
reprintsA joint venture between Stratford Partners and LLJ has acquired a 189-unit apartment complex in northern San Diego County.
The joint venture put down $33.6 million for Pacifica Palms Apartments at 1861 East Washington Avenue in Escondido, according to Institutional Property Advisors (IPA), a division of Marcus & Millichap. The deal works out to about $178,000 per unit.
An entity named Pacifica Palms LLC, run by David J. Snodgrass and Barbara Snodgrass, sold the property, records with PropertyShark show.
The gated Pacifica Palms includes 20 buildings across 8 acres on East Washington Avenue, about 2.5 miles from Downtown Escondido. The development was completed more than 60 years ago.
IPA’s Chris Zorbas and Alexander Garcia Jr. represented the seller and procured the buyer. Zorbas described the property as a rare chance to acquire a large value-add multifamily asset in a supply-constrained submarket.
“The Escondido submarket has seen limited availability of multifamily assets of this size,” Zorbas said in a statement.
Garcia pointed to the widening cost gap between renting and owning, as Escondido home prices have increased 19 percent since 2021, according to IPA.
“The disparity between monthly living expenses for renting versus owning should sustain low vacancy and place upward pressure on Escondido’s rental prices for the foreseeable future,” Garcia said.
San Diego’s multifamily market remains tight, with vacancy at 4.2 percent earlier this year, and average effective rents of $2,832 per month, according to Marcus & Millichap’s most recent multifamily report. Deal flow also improved by 25 percent during the 12 months ending in March. Escondido is among the tighter, more affordable submarkets, where limited vacancy is expected to persist.
Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.

Havas, which creates advertising, public relations and marketing campaigns for health care brands, signed a 15-year deal to renew its existing 189,461-square-foot office at George Comfort & Sons’ 200 Madison Avenue and tack on an additional 64,657 square feet, according to the landlord.
The deal, which stretches through at least 2041, brings the health company’s total footprint to 254,118 square feet across five floors of the 26-story office building seven blocks south of Grand Central Terminal.

By Emily Davis August 27, 2026 2:10 pm
reprintsThe deal-makers at Savills have struck a lease of their own.
The global real estate advisory firm is expanding its New York City presence by taking 20,481 square feet for a satellite office at Rudin’s 560 Lexington Avenue, according to a Thursday announcement by the landlord. Savills will occupy the entire third floor at the 22-story Midtown East tower for a five-year term.
Asking rent for the deal was not disclosed, but the average asking rent for Midtown office space was $84.88 per square foot in July, according to Colliers.
Rudin’s Kevin Daly and Craig Panzirer represented the landlord in-house in the deal, alongside a CBRE team of Brett Shannon, Peter Turchin, Eric Deutsch, Lauren Levy and Jacob Rosenthal. Savills represented itself in the transaction.
Savills’ new office space sits four blocks north of its U.S. headquarters at 399 Park Avenue.
The new lease will accommodate Savills’ program and project management group, a spokesperson for the brokerage told Commercial Observer. The added elbow room comes just a few weeks after Savills completed its acquisition and launch of Eastdil Secured Savills in a major platform expansion.
Situated at the corner of East 50th Street and Lexington Avenue three blocks east of Rockefeller Center, 560 Lexington has attracted more than 110,000 square feet of deals that have now been completed there this year, according to Rudin.
Hedge fund SummitTX Capital took nearly 18,000 square feet across the 19th floor earlier this year, Commercial Observer reported, followed by investment firm Ally Bridge Group’s 6,440-square-foot relocation in May, financial firm Marex’s 39,552-square-foot deal in April, and sports investment firm Dynasty Equity’s 9,910-square-foot lease in June.
Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.

Vivmark Residential Transfers $742M California Multifamily Portfolio from Avalon
The new apartments are approximately 1,843 units within the Vivmark portfolio, which spans more than 180,000 units across the country
By Brian Pascus August 27, 2026 12:58 pm
reprintsFollowing a generational merger, the largest apartment real estate investment trust (REIT) in the business just made things a little more official.
Days after AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential completed their $71 billion merger — the largest merger of publicly traded REITs in history — the new firm, Vivmark Residential, has transferred seven apartment complexes in Northern California near San Francisco, totaling more than 1,800 units, at a value of $741.8 million into the new company.
The Mercury News first reported the transfer to Vivmark Residential, a public entity that now boasts a portfolio in excess of 180,000 rental apartment units.
The properties include Avalon Campbell, a 348-unit complex at 508 Railway Avenue in Campbell, Calif., valued at $147.3 million; Avalon Towers on the Peninsula, a 238-unit complex at 2400 West El Camino Real in Mountain View, Calif., valued at $140.4 million; Avalon Fremont, a 308-unit complex at 39939 Stevenson Common in Fremont, Calif., valued at $124.3 million; Eaves Creekside, a 300-unit apartment at 151 Calderon Avenue in Mountain View, Calif., valued at $117.3 million; Eaves Fremont, a 237-unit complex at 231 Woodcreek Common in Fremont valued at $88.9 million; Eaves Dublin, a 204-unit apartment at 7904 Fall Creek Road in Dublin, Calif., valued at $64.6 million; and Eaves Union City, a 208-unit complex at 2175 Decoto Road in Union City, Calif., valued at $59.1 million.
Brad Dillman, founder and principal of Florey Street Advisors, told CO after the merger was announced that both AvalonBay and Equity had “enormous coastal exposure across both firms,” and that “they overlap in like 95 percent of their geographies.”
Vivmark Residential did not respond to requests for comment by press time
Correction: This was initially reported as a sale, but it was actually a transfer of property into the new entity.
Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialosberver.com.

NJ Transit lost nearly $4 million operating trains for the eight World Cup games at the Meadowlands this summer, despite charging riders a staggering $98 per round trip.
A report on the issued by the agency’s Chief Financial Officer Jacqueline Stamford on Monday said the agency lost $3.8 million to run the trains, but painted the loss as a relative win.
“NJ Transit was able to limit its financial risk and improve farebox recovery through appropriate ticket pricing and prudent budgeting practices, including strategic contingency planning,” Stamford wrote in the memo.
The financial loss was first reported by NorthJersey.com. NJ Transit officials went over the figures during a committee meeting on Friday.
The service was disruptive for many riders who weren’t going to the World Cup. For four hours before each match, the NJ Transit areas of Penn Station were reserved exclusively for people with game tickets. Everyone else was directed to take the PATH train and transfer in Newark.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill and NJ Transit CEO Kolluri had pledged publicly that New Jersey taxpayers would not subsidize transit for the most watched sporting event on the planet. NJ Transit initially set ticket prices for World Cup trains at $150, though that price was later lowered to $98 after more corporate donations came in. The agency also sold a $1.7 million sponsorship that temporarily renamed the Meadowlands Rail Line to the DoorDash Meadowlands Rail Line.
NJ Transit had projected World Cup service to cost roughly $62.5 million, according to the memo. The service ultimately cost about $55.7 million, and the agency took in about $51.7 million in revenue. The agency reserved up to 40,000 round trip train tickets to each game, but ridership peaked at 26,221 on June 16 for the game between France and Senegal.
Stamford’s memo said the agency lost about 7 cents for every dollar spent on the service. The memo notes NJ Transit typically loses about 85 cents on the dollar when serving events at MetLife Stadium, making the World Cup games a win by comparison.
Stamford said the deficit for the World Cup service will be covered by advertising revenue and real estate sales.
“As promised, NJ Transit will neither cut service nor seek additional funds from the legislature this fiscal year to cover the shortfall,” Stamford wrote in the memo.
At the NJ Transit committee meeting Friday, transit officials said that employees were required to work additional hours to staff the World Cup service.
NJ Transit has touted its World Cup performance, saying they handled the equivalent of eight Super Bowls worth of attendees over a 39-day period. The agency said it served more than 370,000 passengers for the matches.
The eight World Cup games at MetLife Stadium, including the tournament’s final match, were largely served by NJ Transit trains and the local host committee’s shuttle buses. Those shuttles ran four routes to the stadium – three from Midtown and one from Clifton. Shuttle bus tickets were sold for $20 round trip.
The host committee said its stadium shuttles carried a total of 116,224 people across the eight games, averaging 14,528 per match.
The stadium was largely inaccessible by car for World Cup games. The only parking available was at the neighboring American Dream Mall, and those spots were sold for up to $300 each.
Ramsey Khalifeh contributed reporting to this story.

Nassau County police are investigating after several people were spotted entering a manhole in Wantagh, Long Island, early Thursday morning.
Department officials said they received calls from witnesses around 1 a.m., reporting the bizarre behavior at the intersection of Wantagh and Jerusalem avenues.
What the people were doing — as well as why they went down the hole in the first place — remains unclear, according to police. Officers who arrived to investigate didn't find anyone in the manhole, and said no witnesses had reported seeing the individuals emerge.
The incident follows a strange series of similar sightings in New York City. A video shared on social media and confirmed by the NYPD shows five people climbing out of a manhole near West 31st Street and Seventh Avenue around 4 a.m. on Tuesday. Some appear to be wearing dark clothing and headlamps.
In May, witnesses observed groups of seven or eight people entering two manholes in Gravesend and Williamsburg – opposite ends of Brooklyn – and emerging hours later.
The NYPD has not made arrests in any of the cases, and says it is continuing to investigate. It’s unclear whether the incidents are connected.
The city’s Department of Environmental Protection warns that entering the sewer system is illegal and that doing so risks exposure to hazards like potentially deadly gases, unstable surfaces and flooding.

sources.retrieved_text:
This column originally appeared in On The Way, a weekly newsletter covering everything you need to know about NYC-area transportation.
Sign up to get the full version, which includes answers to reader questions, trivia, service changes and more, in your inbox every Thursday.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has a $4 billion plan to fix a section of the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway. But how is he going to pay for it?
Here’s an idea that draws inspiration from Robert Moses, the renowned-but-infamous urban planner who built the crumbling triple-cantilever that’s now in dire need of repair: Make drivers cover the cost.
Sara Lind, executive director at the transportation advocacy group Open Plans, said she supported the idea of finding a way for drivers to pay for Mamdani’s highway construction plan.
“The city should explore tools like tolling to reduce congestion, manage demand and pay for car-based infrastructure,” Lind wrote in a statement. “We should be using dynamic tolling around the city, including on the BQE, along with tools like low-emission zones that can mitigate the negative impacts of driving and freight on communities.”
But the administration would face significant obstacles if it sought to institute a new toll to cover the cost of the BQE project.
City officials pointedly said they won’t ask for federal funding to pay for the plan to build a temporary highway along Brooklyn Bridge Park so crews can fix the triple-cantilever beneath the Brooklyn Heights Promenade. The city owns that portion of the highway — and the transportation department wants to avoid the federal bureaucracy that could delay the plan.
Absent federal money, Mamdani’s push to rebuild the 1950s-era highway would presumably rely on subsidies from city and state taxpayers. The cost would be covered by far more New Yorkers than just the 130,000 drivers who use the triple-cantilever every day.
During his tenure as Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority chair, Moses managed to erect bridges and tunnels across the city without major federal subsidies. Instead, he’d take out loans from bondholders to cover construction, and pay off the debt with the money from tolls he charged to use the crossings.
Adding a toll to the BQE would require federal approval, experts said.
“I’m all for pricing motor vehicles but tolling this section, which is designated an interstate, may run afoul of the Interstate Commerce Commission,” said Sam Schwartz, a transportation analyst and former city traffic commissioner. “In the 1980s I tried to ban tandem tractor trailers from this segment of the BQE and was stopped by ICC rules.”
Eric Goldstein, a lawyer for the Natural Resources Defense Council who sued Gov. Kathy Hochul for delaying the start of congestion pricing, said that adding a toll to the BQE to pay for the work would undermine Mamdani's calculated choice to skirt federal approval.
“One of the reasons why the city is doing it this way is so that at this point the federal government doesn't have to be involved,” said Goldstein. “The Mamdani administration's approach making this a city program is designed to cut through years and years of bureaucracy, red tape and challenges that might ensue, at least with the current administration in office in Washington, D.C. Down the line, if that changes, there might be ways of accelerating aid and financial assistance, and that ought to be looked at.”
Other experts were skeptical Mamdani’s plan would get done within his proposed timeline — and warned taxpayers could be on the hook for a lot more than $4 billion.
“I think $4 billion is not a realistic estimate,” said Kaan Ozbay, a professor at NYU’s Tandon School of Engineering. “Given the history of megaprojects in the US, it will be at least double that amount and will most likely take longer than 10 years.”
City officials and experts agree there isn’t much more time to delay. New York transportation planners have been trying to figure out what to do with the crumbling triple-cantilever for 20 years — and they’re running out of time before the structure becomes unstable.
“There is no federal money available and there is no time to wait for a friendlier administration in Washington,” said Schwartz. “It is crumbling, pieces have fallen and are now held up by netting, there have been punctures through the deck that present hazards to drivers and steel reinforcing bars are corroded, weakening the structure. It is just a matter of time before there is a structural failure with potentially catastrophic consequences.”
NYC transportation news this week
LIRR to run direct trains to Montauk year-round. The LIRR offers direct train rides from Penn Station to Montauk during the summer. But during the off-season, riders have to make at least one transfer to get out there. MTA officials said they’ll make a direct 5:13 p.m. train run a permanent part of the weekday schedule starting next month. The MTA said ridership on the Montauk Branch continues to grow, with 1.21 million passengers recorded so far this year, a 6.4% increase compared to the same period last year.
MTA to pilot virtual OMNY cards after a year of delays. The MTA plans to begin testing out a “virtual” reloadable OMNY card that New Yorkers can keep on their smartphones later this year, making life easier for transit riders who rely on physical cards to pay their fares.
Locals are riding the ferry — and the tourist wave — to Red Hook. The ferry has made a difference for the neighborhood’s business owners and arts community.
Safety work begins on one of Jersey City's most dangerous roads. Construction on a stretch of JFK Boulevard near an area heavily used by pedestrians coming and going from the PATH train’s Journal Square station started this week and is expected to last 18 months.
NYPD crackdown on illegal e-bikes cranks up. New police data shows that the NYPD has drastically escalated its crackdown on e-bikes since Mayor Mamdani took office at the start of the year.
Curious Commuter
Have a question for us? Use this form to submit yours and we may answer it in a future newsletter!
Question from Adelia in Brooklyn
The MTA app supposedly tells us when the next bus will arrive. Is it just using a prearranged schedule that drivers are supposed to keep to or is it able to track buses' actual location and speed? In other words, how does it work?
Answer
Each MTA bus has an onboard GPS tracker that allows the transit agency to see live locations of its bus fleet and relay that information to riders. The MTA has defined bus schedules for its drivers — but they don’t always reflect what’s happening on the streets. The new MTA app features location information that is updated every five seconds. The app is excellent and worth downloading.

Dolly Parton has shuffled off this mortal plane, and the world is in mourning. Flags are flying half staff, the Empire State is glowing pink, and there is an across-the-aisle sentiment that we’ve lost an inspiringly empathetic soul who, despite the heights her talent and charisma rocketed her to, maintained a heart of gold and a rhinestone-encrusted north star of kindness.
Various memorial tributes popped up around New York immediately following news of Parton’s death – a mournful bluegrass jam at East Village bar Lucinda’s and a declaration of eternal love on IFC’s marquee – but for those in need of further communal grieving, here are five NYC venues hosting Dolly celebrations this weekend and beyond.
Mark Morris Dance Group
Choreographer Angela Trimbur is leading a Dolly-themed dance class Friday night. The class promises to be a fun but low-stakes full-body workout featuring choreography “designed to make you feel like you’re thirteen years old in a backyard and we are all gonna work on a routine to show our parents before dinner and they will say ‘oh that was…interesting’” according to its Eventbrite. Knee pads recommended.
$29. Friday, Aug. 28, 7pm. 3 Lafayette Av., Fort Greene
Boyfriend Co-op
For a more passive Dolly-mourning experience, Bushwick’s relatively new queer bar Boyfriend Co-op will be playing Parton’s films and music this Saturday, with tissues available “for our collective tears.” Attendees are encouraged to put on a Dolly-approved fit.
Free. Saturday, Aug. 29. 1157 Myrtle Av., Bushwick
C’mon Everybody
A celebration of “all that is Dolly Parton” is coming to Bed-Stuy’s C’mon Everybody on Saturday. The tribute night is set to feature shows by five different performers, including Miss Ma'am She, Rify Royalty and Hanukah Lewinsky. In the name of continuing Dolly’s philanthropic literacy work, organizers will also be collecting donations for a local book drive.
$20. Saturday, Aug. 29, 6:30pm doors, 7pm show. 325 Franklin Av., Bed-Stuy
Cassette
Ridgewood venue Cassette is dedicating their weekly, cover-free drag show this Saturday to Dolly, a natural inspiration who once said “If I hadn't been a girl, I'd have been a drag queen.” Attendees are encouraged to tip performers and wear their best country diva look. Then, this Monday, they’re hosting a live Dolly Parton tribute band, with all proceeds donated to Dolly’s Imagination Library. Finally, on Thursday they’ll be screening a double Dolly feature of “Nine to Five” and “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas.”
Drag show: Free. Sat., Aug. 29, 10pm; live band tribute: $10 in advance. Mon., Aug. 31, 7:30pm; double Dolly feature: Free. Thurs., Sept. 3, 7pm. 68-38 Forest Av., Ridgewood
Arlene’s Grocery
Album listening club Vinyl World has adjusted their programming in honor of Dolly’s death and will be playing the entirety of her 1974 album “Jolene” at Lower East Side standby Arlene’s Grocery this Tuesday. There will also be some classic country vinyl DJ sets throughout the night, and it’ll be capped with a giveaway of a copy of the record. Vinyl World describes themselves as an album listening club of 20-somethings who “meet up to listen to full albums the way they were meant to be heard: on vinyl.”
$10 suggested. Tues., Sept. 1, 7pm. 95 Stanton St., Lower East Side

Ann Blatt has been a New York Liberty fan since day one.
She remembers waiting with friends after each game to get autographs from their favorite players like Liberty Legend Teresa Weatherspoon.
“I saw T-Spoon running up and down the court and said, ‘Ooh, this is fun.’” Blatt said. “I gotta go get me a season ticket."
Just two years after the Liberty’s inaugural 1997 season, Blatt was travelling to watch the team. She followed the Liberty to Houston for an iconic finals game in 1999 where Weatherspoon made a half-court buzzer-beater to win the game. The moment became known as “the Shot.”
Caitlin Shann, who uses they/them pronouns, became a fan just a few years ago. “When [the Liberty] first came to Barclays, it was just the queerest, most loving, supportive, safe place to watch sports,” Shann said. They decided pretty soon to invest in a season-ticket membership, costing them roughly $600 in 2024. But like Blatt, they soon realized prices were going up significantly.
When the WNBA began 30 years ago, the Liberty were one of the league’s original eight teams. Compared to the NBA, the league had a relatively smaller audience, which had the inverse advantage of lower ticket prices to games. If you were a New York basketball fan but couldn’t afford Knicks season tickets, you could find affordable seats if you rooted for the Liberty. Over time, though, the popularity of women’s sports, and of basketball in particular, has grown. The Liberty has also become a highly competitive team; they won the league championship in 2024 and this season marked their sixth consecutive season making the playoffs. As their fanbase grew, so has demand for tickets. Since the team moved to Brooklyn in 2020, the number of season ticket holders has increased more than 900%, according to a Liberty spokesperson.
With higher demand has come higher prices, which some fans say has left them unable to experience the team in the way they once did. Some feel like their loyalty has not been rewarded. Shann said in 2025, they paid over $1,100 for their season tickets. This year, they skipped season tickets altogether for a combination of reasons, including the 40% jump in price. “Raising the prices astronomically, it’s like the gentrification of the WNBA, the gentrification of Barclays,” they said.
A Liberty spokesperson said increasing prices has helped the team continue to invest in players, fan experience, new premium spaces, upgraded food and beverage options and more merchandise. The Liberty do offer season-ticket options starting at $25 per game and cap increases at 25% per year for their longest-tenured season-ticket members, according to the spokesperson.
Morgan Taylor, the Liberty’s vice president of business operations, said there's a seat at every price at the arena. “Even if some people move back a few rows, we make sure that Barclays can remain home for our fans,” Taylor said.
Shann wasn’t satisfied with that response. They say for people with physical disabilities like themself, sitting in the upper bowls is a nearly impossible task. The Liberty spokesperson said elevators help fans with mobility challenges get to any concourse and wheelchair-accessible seating is available on every level, including the upper bowls.
Ann Blatt said she's had to make tough decisions about her fandom. “When I first started, I had three season tickets for my two nieces. Now I wind up having a half a season ticket for that one of the nieces and her son,” Blatt said. Still, she said she’s in it for the long haul. “I go to every game now, I'm going to join next year, no doubt.”
Shann, however, worries her fandom has run its course. “ It’s sad because the W was a little bit of a utopia. Maybe that was just a little naiveté.”

candidates.title: What the Knicks can tell us about NYC's rise in felony assaults
candidates.what_happened:
A crowd throws objects at NYPD officers during New York Knicks against San Antonio Spurs Game 5 of the NBA Finals on June 13, 2026 in New York City. 
  

 Complaints rose 31.4% on the five nights the team played in June's NBA Finals, according to a new Vital City report. [  more ›  ]

sources.retrieved_text:
When the Knicks played, New Yorkers watched. After the games, they started swinging.
Felony assault complaints across New York City were 31.4% higher on the five nights the Knicks played during June's NBA Finals than on comparable nights, a spike that a new midyear report says may offer a window into the city's persistent rise in felony assaults.
The civic policy journal Vital City's midyear report, published Tuesday, found felony assault complaints have risen for six consecutive years, even as major crime overall fell 5.6% in the first half of the year. Murders and shootings also declined.
Felony assault complaints were 48% higher in the first half of 2026 than during the same period in 2019. Two decades ago, they accounted for one in 10 of the NYPD's felony complaints. Now, they account for about one in six, according to the report.
The timing of the complaints on Finals nights closely tracked the games themselves.
The city averaged about 51 felony assault complaints between 7 p.m. and 4 a.m. on NBA Finals nights, versus about 39 on comparable nights. The analysis found overall complaints fell while the games were underway, then climbed after the buzzer, running nearly 39% above normal at 1 a.m.
The pattern held on wins and losses. The largest jump, nearly 50%, came on the Monday the Knicks lost Game 3.
Manhattan, home to Madison Square Garden, outdoor watch parties and many of the bars where fans watched the games, tallied the largest increase, with felony assault complaints more than doubling.
"It really seems to be about a lot of people being out late together rather than about celebration," said Paul Reeping, the report's author. He attributed the broader six-year rise to an erosion of social cohesion since the pandemic.
An NYPD spokesperson pointed to more recent data showing felony assault complaints were down 0.4% through July compared with the same period last year, after falling 6.4% in July. Vital City’s analysis, by contrast, covered the first six months of the year.
The report also found that about 40% of the growth in total crime complaints since 2019 came from offenses heavily influenced by police enforcement rather than from reports by victims or witnesses. Vehicle and traffic offenses alone are up 342% since 2019, according to the report.
Total complaints in the subway have nearly tripled since 2019, but strip out several enforcement-heavy categories and the count is down about 11%.
Liz Glazer, founder of Vital City, said the enforcement approach falls into an old pattern for low-level offenses: "the process is the punishment." Arrests spike, she said, but "huge percentages of those cases" are dismissed at arraignment.
"You've accomplished putting the person in jail and in lockup for a night before they get arraigned, and then the case is over," Glazer said.
But the underlying drivers of fare evasion, shoplifting and trespassing go unaddressed, and the cycle repeats, she said.

candidates.title: NYC eyes new requirements for treatment of pregnant people in police custody
candidates.what_happened:
New York City Councilmember Selvena Brooks-Powers at a City Council hearing. 
  

 The City Council bills were introduced three months after Samantha Randazzo, then nine months pregnant, gave birth to a boy while in NYPD custody in a Brooklyn courtroom. [  more ›  ]

sources.retrieved_text:
New York City could impose new requirements on the NYPD's treatment of pregnant New Yorkers in custody and require police to track children who are present when their parents or caregivers are arrested.
The push comes after a high-profile incident earlier this year when a woman gave birth in a Brooklyn courtroom. The City Council bills were introduced three months after Samantha Randazzo, then nine months pregnant, gave birth to a boy while in NYPD custody after she was arrested on low-level drug and trespassing charges.
Public defenders and legal advocates have said prosecutors could have declined to prosecute the case or a judge could have dismissed it.
The city has previously settled lawsuits with other women who said they were forced to give birth while restrained by officers, including an incident in 2018 when a woman was arrested two days after her due date and went into labor in a holding cell without water.
The Queens elected official behind the newly introduced legislation said she drafted the bills “almost immediately” after she learned of this year’s incident.
“I was instantly just furious at the lack of dignity and respect that was shown to this woman and just the lack of thought from anyone having the thought that this is an emergency situation and that actions need to be taken to get her the proper medical attention,” Councilmember Selvena Brooks-Powers said in a statement. “At the end of the day, she’s still just a person enduring one of the most vulnerable moments in her life.”
The first bill, Intro. 995, would require the NYPD to train officers on laws, rules and policies governing the use of restraints on people in custody who are pregnant or postpartum. It would also require the department to publicly report each year on how many officers received the training.
The second bill, Intro. 996, would require the police department to report quarterly on arrests where a child was present, including the number and ages of the children and whether they were left in the care of another adult.
The legislation is backed by several organizations that advocate for currently and formerly incarcerated New Yorkers and their families, including the Bronx-based Osborne Association.
“When an individual is involved in the criminal justice system there are these ripple effects that benefit all of us to pay attention and to support children who are affected by their parents’ arrest and incarceration,” said Tanya Krupat, the organization’s vice president for policy and advocacy.
The city legislation comes after state lawmakers passed a bill that would restrict the use of restraints on people in police custody who are pregnant, in labor or delivery or within 12 weeks after a pregnancy ends, with limited exceptions.
That bill, which was originally introduced in January 2025, swiftly passed the state Senate and Assembly weeks after Randazzo gave birth in May. The legislation is awaiting Gov. Kathy Hochul's signature.
“We are reviewing the legislation. The Mamdani administration is committed to delivering a criminal justice system that safeguards the health and well-being of all New Yorkers, including those who are pregnant and post partum," Sam Raskin, Mayor Mamdani's Deputy Press Secretary, said in a statement. "We also are dedicated to ensuring that all city agencies take appropriate transparency measures.”

candidates.what_happened:
Bruce Blakeman's event with Trump was held at the Nassau County police academy. Cadets and officers filled the grandstand. 
  

 A complaint filed with the Board of Elections alleges Blakeman improperly exploited his office as county executive. [  more ›  ]

sources.retrieved_text:
Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman’s recent appearance with President Donald Trump at his county’s police academy — with uniformed cadets and officers sitting behind them — amounted to an improper partisan political rally, Democrats allege in a formal complaint expected to be filed Friday with the state Board of Elections.
The Aug. 14 event featured Republican candidates for Congress from around the state. Several spoke from the rostrum, denouncing Democratic officeholders. Blakeman, who is also running for governor, attacked state policies and Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul during his speech.
Trump took the stage and praised his host after discussing new crime figures.
“We have to get Bruce into office,” Trump said before mentioning Blakeman’s Democratic opponent. “Nowhere is the communist attack on American society more clear than in New York state. The radical-left Gov. Kathy Hochul has been very, very bad on crime.”
The rhetoric and choice of speakers effectively made the event a partisan political rally, New York State Democratic Committee Chair Jay Jacobs said. He said Blakeman improperly used the resources of his public office to benefit his campaign by holding the event in a county-owned facility secured in part by county police.
“Candidate Bruce Blakeman, while accepting public finance dollars to mount a campaign, has exploited the governmental office of Nassau County executive to deploy county funds, facilities and personnel, all in furtherance of his own statewide candidacy,” Jacobs wrote in the complaint, which was reviewed by Gothamist.
State law prohibits the use of public resources for campaign activity. Incumbent officials, including both Hochul and Blakeman, often use their official bully pulpits to make points that are later echoed in campaign advertisements and speeches.
In a statement, Blakeman described the Democrats’ complaint as a “Hail Mary.”
“Of course Kathy Hochul would criticize the president for coming to tour our outstanding law enforcement facilities and honor law enforcement professionals,” he said.
Jacobs said it was far more than a tour.
“This was a campaign rally. It looked like a campaign rally. It smelled like a campaign rally. It is a campaign rally. And that's okay, but then a campaign should pay for it,” he said.
The Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Public Citizen filed a federal complaint against U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche for speaking at the event. Public Citizen said Blanche effectively endorsed Blakeman when the attorney general described the candidate as “great” in a speech.
A Department of Justice spokesperson said the complaint was baseless and politically motivated.
The White House billed the gathering as an official event to announce crime statistics. The president subsequently described the event on social media as “a Rally in Nassau County in honor of Bruce Blakeman, who is running for Governor of New York.”
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said that “extreme liberal Democrats” were deflecting attention from “soft on crime policies.”
“President Trump promised to stand with our law enforcement officers and to deliver safer American neighborhoods,” Bis said.

candidates.title: A summer surge in ICE arrests in NYC and NJ, mostly of people with no criminal history
candidates.what_happened: New data confirms a rise in immigration arrests many in targeted communities suspected was underway. [  more ›  ]

sources.retrieved_text:
Arrests by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the New York City area and New Jersey have surged this summer, driven largely by an increase in the number of people arrested without criminal records, according to newly published data.
ICE agents in New Jersey arrested 2,080 people in July, the highest total in at least four years, according to a Gothamist analysis of agency data obtained via records requests by the Deportation Data Project, an academic group. The vast majority — 72% — had no criminal record or pending charges, according to the data.
In the New York City area, ICE agents arrested 919 people in July, nearly double the number arrested in April, the low mark for the year. Over three-quarters of arrestees in July had no criminal history.
While the ICE arrests in the New York City area mark a steep increase, they are no high-water mark. In June 2025, ICE arrested 1,033 people in the city, more than any other month since at least October 2022. There was another ICE arrest surge in the New York City area last fall, peaking in November, when the agency arrested 992 people.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, claimed that the Deportation Data Project “cherry-picked” the data. The spokesperson added that the Trump administration continues to pursue the “worst of the worst” criminals.
The new data confirms what immigration advocates and others have suspected in recent weeks, based in part on an uptick in calls to local hotlines for ICE sightings. The surge in arrests comes as the Trump administration employs new deportation tactics and makes expanded use of other measures.
The tactics include holding mass immigration court hearings where hundreds of cases are held at once, allowing a lapse in funding for immigration lawyers assisting unaccompanied minors, and curtailing humanitarian immigration protections for hundreds of thousands of immigrants, including from Haiti and Syria, previously authorized to remain in the country.
Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, a statewide nonprofit, said in statement that the increase in ICE arrests “is in line with the administration's single-minded focus on a deportation agenda no matter the cost to the American economy or the lives of those caught up in this cruel system.”
“When our neighbors are afraid to go to work, take their children to school, seek medical care, report crimes, or interact with government agencies, it makes all of us less safe and our communities less caring,” Awawdeh said in the statement. “New York must continue to reject the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda and ensure that local resources are not used to facilitate federal immigration enforcement."
Earlier this year, New York state legislators passed new “sanctuary” protections barring police agencies from entering into formal cooperation agreements with federal immigration enforcement, though they stopped short of barring more informal cooperation between local police and ICE.

candidates.title: NYC families get reprieve in fight over trans youths' medical records
candidates.what_happened:
NYU Langone Health in Manhattan. 
  

 Advocates say an appeals court ruling offers relief as the legal fight with the Trump administration continues. [  more ›  ]

facts.name: amount
facts.evidence_span: itment from Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration to funnel $15 million into initiatives providing gender-affirming care for young

sources.retrieved_text:
Transgender New Yorkers and their families say they have some breathing room in their fight to keep their private medical information out of the Trump administration’s hands, but advocates warn the broader battle over their healthcare is far from over.
A federal appeals court this week left in place an order blocking the Department of Justice from obtaining identifying and sensitive health information about young people who received gender-affirming care at New York City hospitals while the government appeals the ruling.
The decision drew praise from local elected officials and LGBTQ+ advocates, who said the immediate protection of patients’ privacy does not resolve broader concerns about access to gender-affirming care in New York.
The dispute stems from federal grand jury subpoenas seeking records from New York City hospitals, including NYU Langone and Mount Sinai, about patients who received treatment for gender dysphoria while they were minors.
The hospitals had said that identifying information would be redacted if records ultimately had to be turned over. But Lambda Legal, the American Civil Liberties Union and the New York Civil Liberties Union filed a lawsuit in June on behalf of several transgender New Yorkers seeking to prevent the disclosure of their identifying and sensitive health information.
“Every family should be able to make healthcare decisions without fear of political interference or exposure,” said Omar Gonzalez-Pagan, senior counsel and healthcare strategist at Lambda Legal. “While this fight is far from over, we are grateful for today’s decision and will continue fighting for the rights and privacy of transgender people and their families.”
City and state officials also applauded the court’s decision.
Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office called the decision “a win for patients” and said New York would continue to defend patients’ privacy against the federal government.
“Donald Trump thinks he can bully our community but he’s wrong,” state Sen. Erik Bottcher told Gothamist on Thursday. “Trans New Yorkers have rights and we’ll fight like hell to defend them.”
Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal said transgender New Yorkers and their families “can breathe a sigh of relief.”
“The Second Circuit got it right: New Yorkers’ private medical records are exactly that — private,” Hoylman-Sigal said. “They should never become political fodder for MAGA lawyers seeking to intimidate young people and interfere with deeply personal health care decisions.”
The Mamdani administration also welcomed the ruling. It filed an amicus brief in June supporting transgender New Yorkers challenging the subpoenas.
“Today’s ruling brings relief to families across New York City. But this fight is far from over,” said Taylor Brown, who heads the Mayor’s Office of LGBTQIA+ Affairs. “We will continue to stand up to the federal government’s campaign to dehumanize transgender people and use every tool at our disposal to protect the rights of transgender New Yorkers.”
LGBTQ+ advocacy groups also celebrated the court decision but cautioned that the city and state should do more to protect access to gender-affirming care.
“This ruling is a welcome rebuke of the relentless campaign of judicial harassment against trans patients, their families and providers,” said Kei Williams, who heads the NEW Pride Agenda, which advocates for LGBTQ+ rights statewide. “But this fight is far from over, and New York’s leaders must meet this moment by protecting access to affordable, life-saving gender-affirming care for every person who needs it.”
Williams pointed to a public commitment from Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration to funnel $15 million into initiatives providing gender-affirming care for young people. The funds would also be used to create a hotline that New Yorkers can use to get real-time information about available resources.
“The court protects privacy but privacy alone does not guarantee access,” Williams continued. “New York needs to move from a kind of offensive posture into building a more durable infrastructure for transgender healthcare.”
The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
This story has been updated with comment from Gov. Kathy Hochul's office.

candidates.title: NYC's suspension classrooms have a major attendance problem, audit finds
candidates.what_happened:
A public school stands on the Upper East Side on August 07, 2020 in the Manhattan borough of New York City. 
  

 A state comptroller audit raised concerns about whether the city's public school students are receiving support after they’re disciplined. [  more ›  ]

facts.name: company
facts.evidence_span: nt was disciplined five times related to weapon possession and use

sources.retrieved_text:
When New York City's school-age students are suspended for serious offenses, they are assigned to spend their time away from school learning in designated classrooms and learning centers. But a new audit by the state comptroller found that more than half the time, they don’t show up.
The audit reviewed suspension and disciplinary data from New York City Public Schools over a four-year period and found high absentee rates among students suspended for more than five days and that many students who have been suspended multiple times are missing out on counseling and other support services.
Low attendance rates at the suspension centers can mean students struggle to catch up when they return to school. When they feel hopelessly behind, they are more likely to drop out, according to the audit.
“My auditors found concerning trends and deficiencies that indicate the need for stronger monitoring and improvements by New York City Public Schools to better support at-risk students,” state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli said in a statement.
“I urge school officials to act on our recommendations to keep these students from falling through the cracks,” he said.
Over the four-year stretch, which spanned the pandemic, the audit also found Black and Latino students on average received longer suspensions than their white and Asian peers for the same infractions.
NYC Public Schools refuted most of the findings in the audit, and said the school system serves more than 900,000 students and is complex. The agency said the conclusions were not representative of the whole school system, which is moving toward a less punitive and more supportive approach to student behavior. In a response letter, the agency said it took the issues raised in the audit seriously.
“We agree with the importance of ensuring consistent disciplinary practices, robust documentation of support, meaningful monitoring of equity and improved outcomes for students who experience disciplinary actions,” NYC Public Schools wrote.
A spokesperson for NYC Public Schools didn’t immediately comment.
The report examined the school years between 2019-2023. Over that span, more than 16,000 students were disciplined two or more times. Those disciplinary actions included teachers removing students from class, principals suspending students for up to five days, and longer suspensions by the superintendent.
The audit stated there was no record that 40% of the students received support or interventions, such as counseling, peer mediation, social-emotional strategies or a behavioral plan. In one case, a student was disciplined five times related to weapon possession and use that resulted in 248 days of being removed from a classroom or the school over the course of a year. There was no record of the student receiving an intervention, the audit said.
Students who receive a superintendent’s suspension lasting longer than five days are supposed to receive instruction at another school or an alternative learning center. On average, these students were absent 54% of the time, according to the audit.
NYC Public Schools said the methodology used by the state comptroller, which used random samples, was flawed. School officials said they have made efforts to improve attendance rates by increasing monitoring and outreach.

candidates.title: Case dismissed against NJ man accused of fatally punching stranger at Penn Station
candidates.what_happened:
Commuters exit a train at Pennsylvania Station in 2017 in New York City. 
  

 Prosecutors say they couldn’t prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the man’s actions were not justified. [  more ›  ]

sources.retrieved_text:
A Manhattan judge on Thursday dismissed the criminal case against a New Jersey man accused by law enforcement of fatally punching a stranger at Penn Station.
The Manhattan district attorney’s office charged Nassadir Tate, 22, with third-degree assault in Eweka Johnson's death on March 14. Prosecutors said Tate punched Johnson one time in the face after a brief verbal argument on the uptown E train platform. Johnson died shortly after.
Prosecutors asked a judge to drop the charge against Tate after reviewing video surveillance, interviewing witnesses, examining an autopsy report and reviewing the defendant’s statement to police. They said they could not disprove beyond a reasonable doubt that Tate’s actions were justified.
“Mr. Tate was faced with a very, very dangerous situation in which he was almost shoved onto the subway tracks without provocation,” Tate’s defense attorney Wayne Gosnell said in a phone call. “He defended himself like anyone else would under the circumstances. He was completely justified in his actions.”
Security footage shows Tate bumping into Johnson as they walked past each other on the subway platform, according to the DA’s office. Johnson then pushed Tate, and the two started to argue. When Tate tried to walk around Johnson, Johnson blocked his path, threw his own jacket to the ground and raised his hands as if preparing to fight, prosecutors said. That’s when the DA’s office said Tate threw a single punch at his face.
According to prosecutors, Johnson remained upright after he was punched and pulled out his phone to call 911. But about two minutes later, after Tate had already walked away, Johnson’s knees buckled and he fell to the floor, the DA’s office said. First responders took Johnson to Lenox Hill Hospital, where he was pronounced dead that evening. An autopsy determined the official cause of death as a ruptured cerebral artery aneurysm following the punch to his face.
In an interview with police, Tate admitted to punching Johnson, according to prosecutors. He said he was afraid for his safety, because Johnson was close to the edge of the subway platform and looked like he was preparing to fight. Tate didn’t learn Johnson had died until his interview with law enforcement, according to the DA’s office.
New York law allows criminal defendants accused of violence to argue that their actions were justified. To do so, they have to establish that they reasonably believed it was necessary to protect them from someone else using physical force against them. They also have to establish that they weren’t the initial aggressor, or they tried to retreat from the situation.
The DA’s office said Tate likely could have established at trial that his actions were justified, and that video surveillance largely corroborates his account of what happened.

Two Brooklyn men were sentenced for staging three car crashes on New York City highways as part of an insurance fraud scheme, Gov. Kathy Hochul and Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz announced Thursday.
Jaime Huiracocha, 53, pleaded guilty to insurance fraud and conspiracy charges and was sentenced to one to three years in prison. Victor Murillo, 34, pleaded guilty to staging a motor vehicle accident as well as insurance fraud and conspiracy charges and was sentenced to two years.
Both men had initially faced up to 15 years when they were arraigned in July 2025.
“Staged auto collisions not only terrify the drivers who are targeted, they put other motorists at risk and ultimately lead to increased insurance costs for all New Yorkers,” Katz said in a statement.
Prosecutors said the two men would recruit people to participate in car crashes by promising them thousands of dollars in payouts.
Murillo drove the cars during the crashes, according to prosecutors, and would slam on the brakes in a deliberate attempt to get rear-ended. In one case, when the driver was able to stop before hitting him, he threw the car in reverse and backed into the driver, according to authorities.
After the crashes, Murillo would exit the car through the passenger side and the remaining passengers would feign being injured, officials said.
Huiracocha trailed Murillo in a separate vehicle, telling him when and how to stage the crashes, prosecutors said. Afterward, he would direct the passengers to go to specific medical clinics, according to officials.
The crashes happened between August and October 2024 on the Belt Parkway near Erskine Street, the Nassau Expressway near Cross Bay Boulevard, and the Belt Parkway in Rosedale. One of the victims helped crack the case open with footage from her dashcam.
In one incident, an insurance adjuster received personal injury claims totaling more than $79,000, according to officials.
Two other defendants have also pleaded guilty and are due for sentencing next month.

The driver of the SUV that crashed on the Belt Parkway Tuesday night — killing him and two friends and injuring four other people — was supposed to be on vacation with his parents overseas, but decided to stay home to fill out his college applications instead, devastated family members said.
Huzayfah Makharesh, 18, was behind the wheel of the black Cadillac Escalade, driving four other teenagers home from dinner in Bay Ridge, according to his uncle Zakaria Algaheim. His parents had offered to take him to Egypt with them for a week, but he declined.
“ He was supposed to go with them, but he said he needed to apply for Brooklyn College,” Algaheim said, adding that he was a “lovely boy” and a great student who was revered by his teachers.
Police officials said the Escalade was in the center lane of the eastbound Belt Parkway around 11:30 p.m. when it had to brake quickly because of a slower car ahead of it, causing a Honda HR-V to rear-end it.
Both vehicles lost control and hit the guardrail along the southern side of the Parkway, and police said the Escalade flipped over – ejecting Makharesh, 17-year-old Konstantin Gerantidi and 16-year-old Abdul Rehman onto the road. They were not wearing seatbelts, the NYPD said.
Another 18-year-old man and a 16-year-old boy from the Escalade were taken to Maimonides Hospital in stable condition, police said. The 46-year-old woman who had been driving the Honda and her 44-year-old passenger were taken to NYU Langone Hospital—Brooklyn in stable condition, where officials said they were also in stable condition.
The three teenagers who died knew each other from their Brighton Beach, Brooklyn neighborhood, where they lived less than a mile apart. Relatives and community members described them all as diligent, respectful and responsible.
Rehman’s cousin, Amir Ramzan, said the teen had been working at the nearby Brighton Beach carnival for the summer.
“ He was a great guy, actually. He was a very hardworking son, very cooperative and helpful to the others… everybody loves him a lot,” Ramzan said, as relatives streamed out of their home on Brighton Fourth Terrace to head to the teen’s funeral on Thursday.
Maksim Nechiporuk, the superintendent at the nearby building where Gerantidi lived with his mother and sister, said he always saw the boy helping with laundry.
“ If we needed a hand around, he would help us,” Nechiporuk said.
He said he hasn’t seen the family since Gerantidi’s death. An online fundraiser to help them pay for funeral expenses had already surpassed $24,000 by Thursday.
”There's nothing you can say that would make someone feel better. ‘I'm sorry for your loss,’ but there's nothing that could describe, like, a death of a child especially,” Nechiporuk said.
Makharesh’s uncle said the family is still waiting for the full police report to provide more details on the crash. Police said Makharesh had a valid license, and said so far it appeared the Escalade was speeding — but they are still investigating how fast the teens were going. The speed limit for that stretch of the Belt Parkway is 50 mph.
“ It's very sad that we lost him,” Algaheim said.

sources.retrieved_text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
If you fail to move your car for alternate side parking in New York City — and get caught — the main penalty is a $65 ticket.
But for many car owners, $65 can feel like a bargain. After all, the five boroughs are home to some of the most valuable curb space in America.
Enter the “shame sticker”: a shield the Department of Sanitation has started slapping on cars violating alternate side parking rules that reads, “This vehicle violated street cleaning rules. As a result, this street could not be properly cleaned.”
The City Council passed a law earlier this year that allowed sanitation agents to start issuing the stickers. They started deploying the stickers earlier this month. But will the measure actually make a difference? Last week, my colleague Elizabeth Shwe hit the streets to find out.
James: First of all, our colleague Brittany Kriegstein reported that when the sanitation department used similar stickers from the late 1980s until 2012, people said they took days to remove and permanently damaged their cars. Are these new stickers any easier to peel off?
Elizabeth: They’re still pretty sticky! Meslin Paulino of Dyker Heights told me she recently saw somebody struggling to take a sticker off their car, but gave up halfway, leaving behind a smudge of white residue. She said she’d start yelling if she saw a sticker on her window and now plans to move her car an hour early to avoid one.
The very bottom of each sticker includes a note that says: “Remove this sticker with warm water and a scraper. Do not litter.” I ran into sanitation supervisor George Jensen, who was putting some of the stickers on cars in Dyker Heights while I was out. He assumes they’re not easy to get off.
James: Is it possible to drive with the sticker on, and wear it like a perverse badge of honor? Or would it block your view and cause you to crash?
Elizabeth: Since they put the sticker in the back window of the drivers side, it doesn’t obstruct the driver’s view. So technically, you can drive with the sticker on and wear it like a scarlet letter if you really wanted to.
James: Do you have any information on where these are being given out? Are certain neighborhoods or blocks that are especially shameful?
Elizabeth: The sanitation department told me Flatbush and Midwood were hit with 247 stickers during the first two weeks of August, more than any other area in the city. Astoria came in second with 212 stickers over that period. The third most-stickered area was Kensington and Borough Park, with 162.
James: Tell me about what you saw in your reporting on this. Where’d you go, who was getting stickered and did you witness any confrontations?
Elizabeth: We went to Dyker Heights early in the morning and saw sanitation supervisor Jensen giving out tickets and putting stickers on a block where five people declined to move their cars for street sweeping. There was one especially bad car that he stickered, which he said hadn’t moved since the winter. It was covered in parking tickets and surrounded by garbage. Jensen said he’s had an eye on that car for a while, ticketing it whenever he’s in the neighborhood. He said he reported the car to DSNY’s Derelict Vehicles Operations unit.
While we didn’t witness any confrontations, Nick Pesce of Dyker Heights told me the stickers cross a line because they vandalize private property. He said it's “just a fight waiting to happen.”
“If I witness somebody putting a sticker on my back, we’re fighting, we’re arguing, and I'm sure the people who put the labels on know it, so they’re watching over their back,” Pesce added.
Jensen told me he hasn’t had aggressive confrontations with drivers yet. Still, he said he gets a little nervous while putting them on.

sources.retrieved_text:
A week after announcing his camera trap had captured the first otter in the Bronx River in a century, a local wildlife researcher was surprised to see a new face in his lens: an American mink.
“It was exciting because it was the first time that I've seen them on my camera traps,” said RJ Hawkins, whose research is overseen by the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Society. “ It's an interesting discovery because like the North American river otter, they're also indicators for a healthy freshwater ecosystem.”
Mink have been spotted in wooded areas of the Bronx before. But the new image is the first official sighting of the feisty predator on this part of the formerly polluted river. The mink joins the otter and a beaver, which all appear to live in the area near the Bronx Zoo. Local nature lovers say the sightings are a testament to nature’s resilience — and the effectiveness of decades of restoration efforts.
“Every species captured by our cameras tells us something about how wildlife is responding to a Bronx River that has become cleaner and healthier after decades of restoration,” said Craig Piper, interim executive director of the Wildlife Conservation Society and director of the Bronx Zoo. “This mink is a reminder that positive progress is the result of the sustained efforts of dedicated organizations.”
By the 19th century New York’s otters, beavers, and mink had been hunted to near-extinction. While their numbers are recovering upstate, they’re still a rare sight in the waters around New York City.
Factories and mills once lined the Bronx River, pumping out products like barrels, bleach and iron. Eventually those factories gave way to the Bronx River Parkway – and the polluted river became a dumping ground.
Growing up in the Bronx in the 1980s, “ you would see cars in the river, tons of tires in the river,” said Javier Lopez, the Bronx River Alliance's interim executive director.
Community groups have organized local clean-ups of the river since at least the 1970s, according to Lopez. “Bronx residents refused to let this river be treated like a dumping ground,” he said.
The Bronx River Alliance and Wildlife Conservation Society scored a major victory in 2011 when they secured over $30 million in federal restoration funds with the help of former U.S. Rep. José Serrano.
They used the money to pull out the junked cars, re-plant the riverbanks, protect more habitat and reintroduce native fish species like alewife, a small, silvery river herring.
“ What we were able to do and what the community was able to do is to give a little bit of respite to nature,” said John Calvelli, the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Executive Vice President for Public Affairs. “And guess what? Nature is incredibly resilient. If we give it some time, it will come back.”
The first furry mammal to return to the Bronx River was a beaver in 2007, which advocates named José, after Serrano. He was joined a few years later by another beaver named Justin Beaver.
The pair disappeared around 2018, according to the Wildlife Conservation Society, likely due to natural causes.
Hawkins, the wildlife researcher, spotted a new beaver on his camera traps last summer, who he’s calling Cardi Beaver. He captured the shot of the otter in June. And now there appears to be a mink – all three animals sharing the same stretch of river.
“The area is a little hotspot of biodiversity in an otherwise very urban landscape,” Hawkins said. “So it's exciting to see just how many species can coexist with us.”

candidates.title: Severe thunderstorms and floods are expected for New York City
candidates.what_happened: Wet weather is expected to clear in time for a relatively dry weekend. [  more ›  ]

sources.retrieved_text:
City officials are warning New Yorkers to be on the lookout for strong storms and heavy rain that might cause some flooding around parts of the city Thursday.
According to the National Weather Service, showers and severe thunderstorms may begin in the late morning, and will continue on and off through the evening, with the greatest chance of wet weather before 11 p.m.
The NWS has issued a flood watch because some of the showers could produce locally heavy rainfall, said meteorologist Brian Ciemnecki.
“ We're mainly looking at the urban and poor drainage flooding in the city that we typically get if we get heavy rainfall — we could experience some of that, that ponding on the roadways, or worse,” he said.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged residents to be cautious.
"The forecast does not currently indicate a widespread flooding event, but thunderstorms can develop quickly and produce heavy rain and strong winds in a short period of time,” Mamdani said in a statement. “Check conditions before traveling, avoid flooded streets and other flooded areas, and stay informed by texting NOTIFYNYC to 692-692."
Officials from New York City Emergency Management are also warning residents not to drive, bike or walk through floodwater, which can hide submerged hazards and electrical dangers. They are reminding those who live in basement apartments to stay alert and be prepared to move to a higher floor if conditions worsen.
The forecast calls for anywhere from .5 – 1.5 inches of rain across the city, with some areas possibly getting 2.5 inches of rain where stronger storms develop. Higher totals are more likely north and west of New York City, with lower rainfall totals expected across southern Brooklyn and Queens, according to the NWS.
Some of the more intense storms also pose the risk of damaging wind gusts of up to 65 miles an hour, and small hail, according to forecasters.
The good news: most of the wet weather will clear out by later in the day Friday, leaving a mostly dry weekend.
“ It looks like we do carry at least a chance of some showers during the day Friday, but it should not be as widespread as what we're expecting today,” Ciemnecki said, adding that there might be an isolated shower later Sunday, “But I don't think, at this point, anything would impact anybody's weekend plans.”
Temperatures from Thursday to Sunday are expected to be in the low-80s.
This article has been updated with new information from the National Weather Service.

It’s back-to-school month for most of the city’s students. Here are some highlights:
BIG EVENTS:

The Central Library is also offering private one-on-one Medical Debt Relief Clinic counseling. You can sign up to talk through your situation one-on-one with a volunteer here. Bring your hospital bill and proof of income, like a pay stub or tax return.
In Queens, the Queens Public Library is inviting patrons to take a new look at our state fruit, the apple. Their exhibit America 250: Apples of New York celebrates the crunchy crop with a look at some of its history, traditions and symbolism. It runs from Sept. 2–30, at the Hillcrest, Elmhurst, Sunnyside, Jackson Heights, Central, Richmond Hill, Fresh Meadows, and Glen Oaks libraries.
And on Sept. 4, teachers can take a night off from prepping for the new school year at the NYPL’s Stavros Niarchos Foundation branch. Extra Credit: Educator Comedy Night features current and former teacher-slash-comedians. Registration closes Aug. 31.
BRANCH EVENTS:
Aspiring actors – and the rest of us who just like to read things out loud with others – take note: Friday afternoons at the BPL’s Leonard Library branch are now the place to be to do Table Reads. The library provides the scripts; you decide how much acting you want to do. The first read will be David Mamet's "Glengarry Glen Ross," followed by a discussion.
If hot peppers are more your thing than dark plays about morality and Chicago real estate, the Paerdegat branch is hosting Haitian chef and cookbook author, Nadège Fleurimond, for an evening of Cooking and Collaging. Fleurimond will teach how to make the spicy condiment pikliz.
Participants are encouraged to bring their own recipes and photos. Interpreters will be provided in both English and Haitian Creole.
In Queens, the Elmhurst and Jackson Heights branches of the Queens Public Library are marking Hispanic Heritage Month with a talk by Steven Alvarez, a professor at St. John's University. He's giving a talk on what he calls "Taco Literacy" — how culinary traditions can shape culture, identity, history and community.
New York Public Library is marking Hispanic and Latinx Heritage Month too. Their Sept. 16 Being Zine: zinemaking and documentary series for adults at the Morrisania branch will feature the 1996 film "Palante, Siempre Palante!" about the Young Lords movement.
FOR THE KIDS:
For little ones, Queens is offering a class on making a suncatcher in Arverne, and a nature walk to get to know the local bugs at the Hunters Point branch. The New York Public Library has bilingual storytime in both English and Spanish at the 125th Street branch. And the Brooklyn Public Library has a four-part series celebrating Ezra Jack Keats, the Brooklyn-born author and illustrator of "A Snowy Day," at the Jamaica Bay branch.
And for school-age kids, both New York Public Library and Queens Public Library are offering some back-to-school-oriented events, with giveaways of backpacks and school supplies.
But that’s not all – the day before school starts for New York City public schools, the Brooklyn Public Library's Gerritsen Beach branch is helping students get their glamour on with a Nail Polish Party. The Library provides polish and stickers; all genders are welcome.
And for those who could use a little puppy snuggle the day AFTER school starts, the Brooklyn Heights branch is hosting an opportunity to de-stress with Sandy the Therapy Dog. Both human and dog snacks will be provided.

Bodega workers in the Bronx and Brooklyn are reconsidering how they protect themselves as police continue searching for a man they say is connected to two fatal shootings this week.
Police identified 31-year-old Jesus Acosta of the Bronx as a man they are seeking in connection with both shootings. MD Yousef, 44, was killed and another man was wounded at a store in Brownsville early Sunday. Two days later, 33-year-old Tayvon Shuler was killed at a South Bronx deli. No arrest had been announced as of Wednesday evening.
The shootings have rattled workers and others around both stores. One worker near the Brooklyn shooting said he has even begun closing early.
Outside 149 Grill & Deli on Wednesday, about nine of Shuler’s friends gathered around a makeshift memorial with dozens of candles, balloons, photographs and bottles of liquor.
Jay Zavtvous, 24, said he had known Shuler for about two years and described him as someone who looked out for people in the neighborhood.
“He was a good guy. He was for the community,” Zavtvous said. “It wasn't about violence. It was about building in the community.”
Police said Shuler was inside 149 Grill & Deli on East 149th Street just after midnight Tuesday when a gunman approached him, fired several times and struck him in the chest. The gunman then took an unknown amount of cash from behind the register and fled, according to police. Shuler was taken to Lincoln Hospital, where he later died.
The Brownsville shooting happened just after midnight Sunday inside American Best Pizza and Wings on Rockaway Avenue in Brownsville. Police said Yousef was shot in the head and a 39-year-old man was shot in the leg. A store co-owner said an unknown amount of cash was also taken from the store during the incident. Both were taken to Brookdale Hospital, where Yousef died. The other man, whose name has not been released, was listed in stable condition, authorities said.
On Wednesday, the store was still closed three days after the shooting. Mohammad Abdul Jalil, a co-owner of the store, said Yousef was an employee and a childhood friend he grew up with in Bangladesh.
“He’s my best friend,” Jalil said. “We are growing together.”
Jalil said he was at home when the wounded employee called him. He rushed to the store and found police there. About an hour and a half later, he said, police told him his friend had died.
At a nearby store, 28-year-old Mohammed Ali said Yousef would stop in as a customer. Ali said the killing has made him more aware of working late.
“If I see that places are quiet, like the streets are quiet, and my guts tell me to close, I just close immediately,” he said. “I don’t wait for a second moment.”
The FBI is now offering a reward up to $25,000 for information that leads to Acosta's arrest and conviction. The United Bodegas of America said it is offering a $10,000 reward for information. The group also called for more panic buttons in bodegas and legislation that would allow trained and licensed bodega owners and workers to carry firearms.
“Give us protection, panic buttons and the legal ability to defend ourselves, and impose a mandatory three- to five-year prison sentence on anyone convicted of carrying an illegal gun. We cannot wait for another deadly shooter who does not care about human life,” UBA President Radahmes Rodriguez said in a statement.
The group plans to hold a news conference Wednesday night outside the Bronx deli where Shuler was killed.
Jalil said Yousef came to the United States about three years ago while his wife and two daughters remained in Bangladesh. He said the man loved soccer and cricket and regularly played chess with his roommates.
“I’m very bad. I can’t explain to you,” Jalil said. “I lose him. I can recover? It’s not possible.”
This story has been updated with additional information.

Cortland Offloads 812 West Palm Beach Apartment Units for $208M
The Portofino Place east and west apartment community in West Palm Beach sold for a combined $208 million in two deeds. Cortland Partners sold the 812 apartments at 4400 and 4600 Portofino Way to Fairfield Residential. It comes out to $246,000 a unit.
The S. Florida Business Journal reports the individual properties were valued at $108 million for the first 416 units, built in 2003, and $100 million for the second 396 units, constructed in 2006. Walker & Dunlop, through Freddie Mac, provided the buyers with mortgages of $93.13 million and $85 million, respectively, with a due date in September 2033.
The two apartment complexes last traded for a combined $229 million in 2021.
The two garden-style apartment complexes total a combined 1.13 million square feet. They are situated on 39.2 acres, including a lake. Units in Portofino Place range from 820 to 1,672 square feet and rent from $1,749 to $3,135. Amenities include pools, a media room, a basketball court, a pickleball court, a tennis court, and a fitness center.

BGO, Alliance Industrial Acquire 266K-SF FW Warehouse
BGO and Alliance Industrial Company acquired Northwest Commerce Park Building 2.
