Office Leads Pricing Gains as RCA CPPI Inches Up in July 2026
U.S. commercial property prices edged higher in July as the RCA CPPI US National All-Property Index posted its slowest annual gain since January 2025, MSCI Real Assets reported. The index increased 0.2% from a year earlier and rose 0.1% from June, translating to an annualized growth pace of 1.2%.
“Borrowing costs for commercial real estate show no sign of easing, as the Federal Reserve held its policy rate steady in a divided vote and its chair ruled out any softening of the inflation target,” reported MSCI. “Investors now see scant chance of a near-term rate cut, keeping financing conditions tight across the market.”
By property type, CBD office was the best performer, with prices up 9.9% from a year ago and 1.6% from June. Suburban office pricing also increased, up 4.0% annually and 0.4% from the previous month. The other major property sectors experienced annual declines, ranging from 0.9% for retail to 4.4% for apartments. July marked the ninth consecutive month of annual declines for apartment pricing.

Ogilvie Partners Trades Fort Collins Warehouse Portfolio for $42M
Ogilvie Partners sold the Prospect Innovation Campus, a 226,000-square-foot industrial, flex and research-and-development portfolio in Fort Collins, Colorado, to ZS Capital Partners for $42 million. The campus comprises 11 buildings across four sub-portfolios — Midpoint 3, River Center, Spring Creek and One Prospect — and represents a significant, well-located asset in Northern Colorado’s Front Range industrial market.
The acquisition was ZS Capital Partners fifth industrial acquisition since late 2023 and its largest investment to date, expanding ZS’s Colorado Front Range industrial holdings to approximately 460,000 square feet.
Constructed between the late 1980s and early 2000s, Prospect Innovation Campus offers a functional mix of small-bay industrial, flex and R&D space. Flexible suite configurations and a blend of office and warehouse components allow the portfolio to serve a wide range of users.
CBRE represented Ogilvie in the transaction The team included Jeremy Ballenger, Tyler Carner, Patrick Devereaux, James Brady, and Campbell Davis.

CRE Liquidity Is Closing the Gap Between Capital and Deals
JLL’s recently released Global Bid and Credit Intensity Indices shows that credit markets are supporting transaction velocity, investor conviction is overcoming macroeconomic uncertainty and lenders continue competing to place capital.
The gap between the indices peaked in May 2026 and has steadily narrowed since, “indicating stronger alignment between financing availability and transaction execution,” JLL said.
Investor Implications
Here’s what the data means for investors:
Open liquidity window. Capital markets have moved beyond recovery and into expansion, JLL said. Buyers are benefiting from competitive financing terms that remain historically attractive despite recent yield movements. At the same time, sellers are seeing more investors with greater certainty of deal execution.
Better borrower leverage. Increased lender competition is creating “tangible advantages in deal structuring, pricing and terms,” JLL said. Despite recent increases in Treasury and bond yields, the cost of capital and overall credit environment remain favorable.
Sustainable market alignment. Liquidity and sales markets are becoming better aligned, creating a functionally healthier market. “Buyers can underwrite with greater confidence in financing execution,” JLL said, while sellers start transactions with deeper bidder pools. Lenders, meanwhile, are able to originate loans with greater visibility into refinancing strategies.
What to Look for in H2 2026
JLL described current conditions as a “rare combination” of deep liquidity, competitive financing and motivated buyers and sellers. The Bid and Credit Intensity indices suggest that this environment could persist through the end of the year.
Still, macroeconomic pressures remain. “Decisiveness will increasingly differentiate successful execution from missed opportunities,” JLL said.
Investors should watch whether the weight of available capital continues to offset elevated bond yields, how sector-specific cap-rate adjustments evolve as underwriting is recalibrated.
Investors should also keep an eye on whether yield volatility creates new divergences between credit and investment-sales markets.
Photo: SofikoS/Shutterstock
- ◦Financing

Federal authorities with the Department of Housing and Urban Development seized records and confiscated cellphones from a prominent Plano-based general contractor this week.
Cadence McShane Construction Co. Executive Vice President Srinath Pai Kasturi confirmed to the Austin Business Journal that officers from HUD entered the company’s offices in Austin, Plano and San Antonio to obtain records related to a previous project. That project is subject to litigation following a complaint from a former Cadence McShane employee.
Authorities left the Cadence McShane offices with several boxes and the cellphones.
Cadence McShane is reportedly involved in a whistleblower suit against San Antonio’s public housing authority, Opportunity Home. The company's employees Randall Molnar and Andrea Hughes alleged the company overcharged the U.S. government for construction of a multifamily project in Converse, the San Antonio Business Journal reported.
The firm allegedly exceeded the $7M profit threshold mandated for the job, as HUD limits a contractor’s profit on low-income housing projects to 10%. Cadence McShane employees alleged the company recorded a 17% profit and said they refused to submit fraudulent change orders as instructed.
The contractor claims Opportunity Home is overreaching with its request for records unrelated to the apartment project. Cadence McShane also alleged that the San Antonio housing authority is seeking to claim nearly all of the project’s $7M in profits.
Molnar is no longer employed by the firm, according to the SABJ.
Cadence McShane didn’t immediately respond to Bisnow’s request for comment on the raid of its offices and the Opportunity Home lawsuit.
HUD also didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Kasturi told the ABJ that the Department of Justice said it wouldn’t pursue the “substantive allegations” against Cadence McShane. The DOJ didn't immediately respond to Bisnow’s request for comment.
“We feel very strongly the whole matter is without merit but we have to go through the process,” Kasturi said of the ongoing litigation. “We take pride in our long-standing relationship with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, built through years of close collaboration.”
He said the firm has a track record of delivering HUD-financed affordable housing projects and it remains committed to that work.
In North Texas, Cadence McShane built the 327-unit Flynn at Live Oak multifamily project in the Lower Greenville area of Dallas and worked on the 130K SF Anthology of Highland Park senior living facility near downtown.

“Credit and loan markets are showing few signs of policy restraint,” Warsh told the audience in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Friday morning. “Certain sectors like housing and agriculture are showing strains, but on balance, I would be hard-pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive.”
In his first major speech at the top of the central bank, Warsh also offered his views on the impact of artificial intelligence on the economy and an argument against the forward guidance that has been part of Fed communications since the Global Financial Crisis.
The speech solidified Warsh’s position as an inflation hawk, as the chairman promised again to deliver price stability. For commercial real estate owners and investors, it is the latest and clearest signal that the Fed isn’t inching toward rate relief.
Warsh said the central bank had done a good job on the employment side of its dual mandate but still had work to do to bring inflation down to the Fed’s longtime 2% target rate.
The U.S. lost 23,000 jobs in July, well off economists' forecasts of roughly 83,000 new jobs, but the unemployment rate ticked down slightly to 4.1%. Job growth has been uneven in the last two years, with job losses in seven of the last 20 months, according to an NBC News analysis.
Warsh said that labor markets always have areas of concern, with recent graduates facing hurdles today, but the current market remains robust.
“They may well be concerned about future labor disruptions,” he said. “But as of now, I believe the labor markets are broadly consistent with full employment.”
Warsh, 56, outlined the principles guiding his policymaking inside the Fed, including a view that short-term interest rates are the central bank’s “predominant tool” to achieving its dual mandate.
He complained that “yesterday’s news has a way of getting mistaken for what's happening right now,” and he pledged to lead a central bank that was quieter and more purposeful in its communications.
The comments were in line with criticisms Warsh, who worked at the Fed during the GFC, had leveled against the central bank under then-Chair Jerome Powell. Warsh previously called for structural reforms inside the central bank, and he launched five task forces after he took over that are reviewing practically every aspect of Fed operations.
Warsh has been critical of the forward guidance offered after each Federal Open Market Committee meeting, arguing that the central bank risked tipping investor decision-making by telegraphing its moves ahead of time and before financial conditions supported them.
“We should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade,” Warsh said Friday. “If markets rely materially on the Fed's guidance and the Fed relies on market prices, we're more likely to be blinded to new developments.”
On price stability, the other side of the Fed’s dual mandate, Warsh conceded that “the numbers are more concerning,” but he reiterated that he was committed to pulling inflation down.
“Inflation is running above our 2% target, so the Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices,” he said.
He described the economy as at a “hinge point in history” as artificial intelligence redefines the typical roads to economic growth. The technology remains nascent, and a host of unanswered questions will define how AI broadly remakes the economy, he said.
Warsh raised questions about whether AI’s adoption would result in a significant and sustained boost to productivity, how much competition would exist between leading AI models, and where capital would settle between materials providers, chipmakers, AI-model operators, energy producers and cloud infrastructure providers.
The chairman said businesses were rapidly increasing their capital expenditures while profit margins were at historical highs. Investors are looking for growth in both earnings and outside investment, and credit spreads on corporate bond issuance remain strong.
“I'm impressed by the overall performance of the economy, which appears to have strengthened,” Warsh said.

candidates.title: Bridges Real Estate Snaps Up Mixed-Use Building In Utrecht
candidates.what_happened: Bridges Real Estate acquires prime Utrecht building, boosting city development.

sources.retrieved_text:
Bridges Real Estate has purchased a mixed-use building in the center of Utrecht, as the real estate owner and developer continues to invest in select locations that offer potential for long-term value creation.
Located at Vredenburg 17-19, it offers 6,300 square meters of lettable space across retail, leisure and business uses, with tenants including fashion retailer Bomont, Dutch Gym and Meeting Center Vredenburg.
As part of family office De Wereld van Vermaat, Bridges purchased the building from Redevco for €17.3M, VGvisie reported.
Situated in a high-footfall area of the city center, only part of the building is used for retail, a shift that's becoming increasingly common in city centers across the country. Less than 80,000 of just over 205,000 commercial premises within shopping areas in the Netherlands are now shops, down from 107,000 20 years ago, according to data from market research firm Locatus.
The total has declined for 10 consecutive years as more stores close, while the total of hospitality, leisure and business services units has hardly changed.
But retail is not necessarily struggling. On the contrary, retail turnover increased 3.1% year-over-year in the second quarter of 2026, with nonfood retail up 3.5% as retail bankruptcies dropped to 59, the lowest in three years, according to CBS, the government's national agency of statistics.
And retail in Utrecht is improving at a faster pace. Retail vacancy in the city center dropped from 8.7% to 5.3% by floor space in 2025, close to the 5% vacancy standard, as the amount of retail floor space in use increased for the first time in years, according to the Utrecht Monitor retail report.
Vredenburg in particular is a prime location, as it links the train station to the city’s historic center. The street is also the city’s most expensive shopping street, with rents at €1,350 per square meter in 2025, higher than Rotterdam’s Lijnbaan and only surpassed by Amsterdam’s Kalverstraat.
Guido Aben, real estate director at Bridges Real Estate, said the company can add more value to the building through active management and attention to how it is used.

sources.retrieved_text:
Midsized real estate firms control huge swaths of commercial real estate. There's just one problem — they are underfunded.
A new report from KKR & Co. states that middle-market CRE sponsors — those with at least 25 properties and less than $1.5B in dry powder — control $5.1T of U.S. real estate but have specialized capital needs that aren’t available in off-the-shelf formats.
"The point isn't that these groups can't afford something,” said Ira Shaw, one of the report's co-authors and a partner at Arctos Partners, which is part of KKR's new global investing business. “It's more that those types of capital providers are not available.”
Middle-market players are caught up in conflicting market forces. Historically low sponsor formation and institutional lenders' desire to diversify could push more money their way, but a renewed focus on income through operations rather than cap rate compression is making smaller firms with less economy of scale less appealing.
Using Preqin and CoStar data, KKR found that around 5,800 middle-market sponsors control more than 24B SF worth around $5.1T.
That represents around 85% of the institutionally sponsored market and almost a quarter of the broader CRE sector.
In comparison, 27 large-cap sponsors control around $600B of gross property value. The company identified the large-cap investors as publicly traded multistrategy groups with more than $1.5B in dry powder and then filtered by assets under management through Preqin.
While financing is plentiful in private equity, that's not the case when looking to capitalize general partners for real estate.
“Large institutions have a hard time deploying efficiently below about $25M, so assets below end up raising from the retail channel or from subinstitutional buyers like family offices and regional insurers,” said Ibis Capital Managing Partner Kevin Van Hoesen, an investment adviser and asset manager.
Middle-market investors and developers rely on joint ventures, programmatic partnerships, personal capital and transaction-specific relationships with capital allocators rather than closed-end fund structures.
Midsized firms may benefit from a shrinking investment world. KKR's data shows sponsor formation surged after the Global Financial Crisis. About 2,500 CRE sponsors were formed between 2010 and 2019, nearly 60% higher than the amount founded during the previous decade.
That is partially due to the low-rate environment that preceded it and the lower barrier to entry for real estate versus private equity, Shaw said.
But since 2020, only about 800 sponsors were created. That's the lowest level this century.
That drop has led institutional capital to focus on less experienced real estate managers.
And giants like KKR, Blackstone, Brookfield and BlackRock are expanding into new markets to try to grow their assets under management. KKR said deploying capital to middle-market CRE firms will help accomplish that goal.
"There's a way for institutional capital to serve these sponsors, and that opportunity, and need for it, is magnified by the current environment,” Shaw said.
But even as sponsors scale, capital remains scarce beyond one-off joint venture deals.
Platte Canyon Capital, a middle-market firm that specializes in value-add multifamily investing, has faced challenges accessing capital. The firm pursues distressed assets that are trickier to capitalize.
“The goal post for capital is constantly moving,” Platte Canyon CEO Brennen Degner told Bisnow. “We have a very specific thesis and a bit of a contrarian play that we're pursuing, and I think that's made it even more challenging.”
Platte Canyon seeks basis resets of greater than 50% off-peak, and the underwriting still doesn't always pencil.
Even for the groups willing to engage, Degner said seller expectations remain well above where equity will deploy.
It’s also proven challenging for many sponsors to find institutional investment for their companies.
“That is even more difficult to source than capitalizing individual deals,” said Shlomi Ronen, managing principal of real estate merchant bank Dekel Capital Inc.
One middle-market sponsor that attracted an institutional investor is LCN Capital Partners.
The 15-year-old investment manager was acquired by Goldman Sachs earlier this month in a deal worth up to $410M. But company officials said the only thing that will change for the firm is the scale of its ambition.
By combining with Goldman, “we can better serve our investing and tenant partners at a scale no independent firm could match,” LCN co-founder Edward LaPuma said in a statement.
Platte Canyon has also had success with institutional investors, with Degner calling it more scalable and efficient than raising deal by deal. But the firm is mostly seeking acquisition-limited-partner equity, which has proven hard to find.
Where sponsors once secured multiple equity term sheets after tying up a deal, they now need a strong capital partner upfront.
“You need to know who the partner is going to be before or during the bid process,” Degner said. “Deals are tough to get done when you expect to find the equity afterwards.”
The market may become even tougher for middle-market investors looking for big money. Many of the sponsors formed between 2015 and 2021 were underwriting cap rate compression and cheap debt, not operations.
“That stopped being attractive when rates significantly moved,” Van Hoesen said. “Operating skill has to be underwritten now, and that shrinks the number of deals that pencil.”
Capital competition has intensified, and artificial intelligence deals have drawn investment away from the middle markets.
That’s a structural change, but there’s also a cyclical element that’s affecting the middle markets.
The cost of things like fund administration, audits, compliance and reporting has pushed the minimum viable project size up considerably.
“The shops that used to trade in lower middle-market deals have to chase bigger ones, which means bigger checks, which makes the raise harder,” Van Hoesen said. “That’s the spiral.”

sources.retrieved_text:
After driving a New York City taxi for nearly 20 years, the last trip Richard Coulibaly will take is home to Ivory Coast for his own funeral.
The cabbie’s return to the West African country he left three decades ago grew out of the New York Taxi Workers Alliance and fellow Ivorians tapping into a grassroots social media network to track down his relatives and raise at least $7,500 to help cover the journey and funeral expenses.
The union and police said Coulibaly was found dead at the wheel of his parked taxi in Harlem — not far from where he lived alone in a rented single room — around 5:30 p.m. on July 2, during a heat wave marked by the city’s first 100-degree day in more than a decade. The city’s Office of the Chief Medical Examiner said his cause of death remains under investigation.
His younger brother Christophe Coulibaly, 65, told The City Reporter he had not seen Richard since he left Ivory Coast for the United States in 1996, but the two kept in touch by phone and last spoke a week or two before he died. Yet, Christophe said he was unaware his brother was a cabbie until others informed him after his death.
“He told me he was doing other things,” the 65-year-old said in French in a phone interview this week.
He added that he was surprised to learn of his brother’s demise through the outreach from New York because he hadn’t seemed sick. The NYPD identified Richard as 68 years old, while his brother said he was 73.
“Was it too hot, did that have an effect on him?” Christophe said. “I really don’t know everything that happened.”
The father of four’s remains are set to be shipped in the coming days to the city of Abidjan, according to the Taxi Workers Alliance. As his loved ones await more details about when his body will arrive, Christophe said he is grateful to those who have pushed to return his brother to the family’s home village for burial.
“They have bled themselves dry, they have made an effort,” he said. “May God bless them and may their souls sanctify us for everything they have done.”
A Yeoman’s Effort to Find His Family
The search to locate Coulibaly’s relatives began taking shape in the hours after he was discovered in his cab at Frederick Douglass Boulevard and 116th Street.
“We started to get phone calls from drivers, like one who called and said, ‘I see a taxi pulled over, a lot of police there, an ambulance, looks like a driver died in his taxi,’” recalled Bhairavi Desai, executive director of the Taxi Workers Alliance. “So I went out there with another of our members.”
While they were initially unable to learn the man’s identity or get access to his phone from police because they weren’t next of kin, Desai said they confirmed Coulibaly’s name through a Queens taxi-medallion management company he worked with.
Connecting with his family in West Africa, however, presented a complex challenge that played out over several days. The cabbie’s last name provided a clue as to the southeastern region of Ivory Coast where some of his relatives live, but offered little else in the way of information.
The search was also hindered by Coulibaly’s largely solitary lifestyle, according to those involved in the endeavor.
Aboubacar Diakité, a Harlem small business owner whom Coulibaly had befriended over the years, acknowledged the cabbie led a “difficult” life centered around his job and would “start to cry” when he talked about his family.
“He just go home, sleep, come back to work,” said Diakité, who came to know Coulibaly after doing his taxes. “He was working, working, working, working, every day working.”
“He was isolated, his life was closed,” said Abdul Traore, 52, a fellow taxi driver who did not know Coulibaly but served as a contact to the Ivorian community and consulate.
Still, his last name was enough to start a search through Facebook and WhatsApp groups.
“I wrote a big note saying, ‘OK, we have a brother who just passed away in his yellow cab, and we wanted to know if anybody knows about his family or their whereabouts, they can contact me,’” said Saibou Sidibé, a one-time Uber driver from Ivory Coast. “I gave my phone number.”
Within days, he said, he received a call from a woman in the Washington D.C. area who turned out to be Coulibaly’s niece. Desai said the woman’s boyfriend had spotted a Facebook post about the driver’s death and flagged the last name for her.
“She said, ‘This picture looks like my uncle, so I want to confirm with you if this is him,’” Sidibé said. “I told her, ‘OK, I don’t have enough information, but I have his phone number. So if it’s your uncle, maybe you might know his phone number if he used to call you back home.’”
Sidibé said he heard back from her soon after the call ended, confirming the family connection. Then, he connected with Christophe Coulibaly to begin charting Richard’s long trip home.
‘This Is a Situation No One Will Forget’
An estimated 5,700 Ivorians live in the city, according to city Planning Department data. Among the 180,000 drivers licensed by the city’s Taxi & Limousine Commission, 1,179 — or just over a half-percent — identify their native country as Ivory Coast, TLC numbers show.
“It’s such a small community here, it truly was a needle in a haystack,” Desai said. “We are so grateful that there was a miracle that we were able to reach the family.”
Sidibé praised the Taxi Workers Alliance’s follow-through on a goal that seemed unlikely in the immediate wake of Richard Coulibaly’s death.
“This is a situation no one will forget,” he said. “When you pass away, we know how hard it is for people here, especially immigrants who know nobody. It’s luck, because some people pass away and the body’s there at the hospital, but nobody claims it.”
“This is the sad part of the story in the United States. Sometimes you’re by yourself and you’re just here to work and take care of your family,” Sidibé added.
Christophe Coulibaly said his family will set a date for his brother’s burial once his remains return home.
After that, Christophe said he will write a letter to “infinitely” express the family’s appreciation for everyone who helped Richard come back to Ivory Coast.
“Thank you to all the communities, all the religious communities, all the professional communities,” the younger brother said. “Thank you to the population, everyone who made an effort to gather the money to transfer his body to Abidjan.”

The release of a citywide strategy for building 2,100 public bathrooms will be delayed after Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s team said the task is too complicated to meet its deadline.
The legislation, dubbed the Bathroom Bill, passed the City Council in April 2025 and set out to create a comprehensive plan to double the number of public restrooms by 2035. Each relevant agency was supposed to file an updated strategic plan to maintain the network of loos by Sept. 1, with updates every four years.
But Deputy Mayor Julia Kerson sent a letter on Aug. 12 to Speaker Julie Menin saying they’re backed up.
“Given the extensive cross-agency coordination required to establish a reporting framework, compile baseline data, and develop a substantive strategy toward the law’s target of 2,120 public bathrooms citywide, I am writing to inform you that the report will be submitted after the September 1 deadline,” she wrote.
MORE: Prefab Potty Hyped as Fast and Cheap Is Years Late, Will Cost NYC $3.5M
The mayor’s team has, however, started work on the ambitious plan — including “an interagency working group” and site recommendations.
City Hall hopes to submit the report by Nov. 1, Kerson wrote.
City Councilmember Sandy Nurse (D-Brooklyn) introduced the package of bills last year to find easier, cheaper ways to add more quality bathrooms across the city — and was looking forward to the upcoming report.
There are currently 1,066 public bathrooms in the city, and 943 are open year-round, Nurse said.
“People don’t realize there’s no particular agency or mayoral office tasked with bathrooms,” she told The City Reporter. She and some other councilmembers representing Brooklyn were briefed this month by City Hall on some of the newest bathrooms for their borough.
MORE: Mamdani Pitches New Public Toilets While 50 Park Bathrooms Sit Closed
Nurse said she hopes the report can identify inventive and inexpensive ways to add more public bathrooms.
“What are the new models coming out? What are places across the country, across the planet, what are they doing?” she said. “What are we doing to decrease the cost and cut down on red tape?”
Mamdani in January announced a request for proposals to build modular public bathrooms across the city. In June, the administration announced it had selected Throne Labs Inc. to install and maintain 17 modular public bathrooms. The $4 million pilot program will be overseen by the city’s Economic Development Corp.
“My administration is committed to closing the gaps in this public health infrastructure,” Mamdani said in a statement at the time, “and delivering a network of restrooms that are clean, accessible, and most importantly, close by.”

A year ago, former Mayor Eric Adams launched a sweeping, and costly, new plan to bridge the digital divide in the city’s public schools: purchasing 350,000 new Chromebook laptops equipped with free T-Mobile internet service.
The four-year contract, set to cost the city nearly $330 million, aimed to help schools with large shares of low-income and homeless families whose students lacked internet access outside of school.
But a year into the contract, Adams’ successor, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, is canceling the T-Mobile internet service portion of the contract, which costs the city roughly $3.5 million per month, officials said Thursday. Over the full four years of the contract, the internet service was expected to cost around $200 million.
Mamdani’s administration, which is looking to cut costs amid a multibillion-dollar budget deficit, said the city was paying for more internet coverage than necessary and could secure internet service for students who need it at a lower cost. Officials didn’t immediately say how much they expect to save.
The T-Mobile contract “duplicated existing resources at an unnecessary cost,” Education Department spokesperson Nicole Brownstein said. “By discontinuing this component of this contract, we are saving taxpayer dollars while continuing to deliver the internet connectivity we know our school communities rely on.”
The move also comes amid a growing backlash against the reliance on technology in city classrooms. Critics, including some parents and educators, say screen time has become too pervasive, detracting from learning.
Even before the city inked the T-Mobile contract, an existing program allowed principals to secure LTE service for students who need it for $10 per student per month, Education Department officials said. Officials said that service comes through Verizon, and can add internet to any school-issued Chromebooks or iPads.
Officials notified principals Thursday that the T-Mobile student data plans will end Aug. 31. They asked school leaders to compile lists of students who need internet access and purchase service through the Verizon program by the start of school on Sept. 10. Officials said they have already purchased all 350,000 Chromebooks and distributed them to schools, but didn’t say how many were given to students or how many students were using the internet service.
Several principals, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, described mixed experiences with the massive internet-enabled laptop distribution.
At one Manhattan high school, about one in five students used the new devices and relied on them to connect to the internet at home, according to the school leader.
The principal worried that ending the T-Mobile contract would shift more costs to the school’s budget.
But at a Brooklyn high school, dozens of the computers sit unused in a storage room.
“It’s a tremendous waste,” the principal said, adding that students prefer to access the internet through their phones. Plus, the school has shifted away from using Chromebooks during class because of concerns that an overreliance on technology was getting in the way of student learning, the principal said.
Some officials and lawmakers began expressing concerns about the T-Mobile contract in the months after it was signed, New York Focus reported last December. One official told the outlet that the city did not approach competing wireless providers, and was stuck paying a flat fee for the service regardless of how many students used it.
Lawmakers also worried the city was paying for internet service for far more students than needed it. A state Education Department survey from 2020 estimated that about 13% of the city’s public school students lacked sufficient internet at home, according to New York Focus. The city’s public schools currently enroll about 793,000 K-12 students, meaning about 104,000 would lack internet if the 13% estimate held.
City officials said in 2025 that about 30% of households, containing around 2.5 million residents, did not have both home broadband and mobile internet access. City officials have separately launched efforts to improve Wi-Fi in homeless shelters.
Adams said the T-Mobile school internet deal was funded in part by savings the city made through another deal that made T-Mobile the city’s major service carrier.
The Education Department spends roughly $13 billion a year on contracts, and Mamdani has identified the agency’s contracting — and particularly its spending on student devices — as ripe for cost-cutting.
Officials said the T-Mobile contract was approved by the Panel for Educational Policy, which oversees Education Department contracts, but was held by the city’s Office of Technology and Innovation.
City officials purchased and distributed some 725,000 devices for students during the COVID pandemic but have not tracked how many of those devices remain operational.
Gov. Kathy Hochul, who instituted a statewide bell-to-bell cellphone ban last school year, is considering imposing limits on screen time for younger kids. The Education Department is revising its artificial intelligence guidance for schools and has barred schools from purchasing new software until the guidance is finalized.
Michael Elsen-Rooney is a reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Michael at melsen-rooney@chalkbeat.org.

sources.retrieved_text:
Last Sunday, 87 Vanderbilt University students moved into their rooms at the Nashville university’s new campus in Chelsea, pioneers in the school’s plan to establish an outpost in New York City that will offer a semester away for undergraduates and create a new graduate program in technology and business.
Vanderbilt has committed to spending $44 million on a 99-year lease for the 13 Gothic-style buildings around the leafy quad of the General Theological Seminary of the Episcopal Church. Current renovations on the campus — located a block from the High Line — will cost it about $50 million, with millions more to update additional buildings.
“Our students were telling us for several years now that they wanted to be in New York City,” said James Kellerhouse, the assistant chancellor recruited to get the outpost off the ground. “We knew that because we were recruiting them from New York but they were coming back here after graduating.”
The headlines about the state of higher education in the United States have been dire. “Once globally prominent, U.S. universities are sliding into decline,” proclaimed a headline in the Hechinger Report earlier this month. Even well-known liberal arts colleges like Hampshire College are closing.
Closer to home, the New School, in Greenwich Village, has offered buyouts, laid off 60 professors and staff and closed several academic departments in an effort to close a $50 million deficit. In Gramercy Park, the School of Visual Arts has seen enrollment drop by more than 30% since 2017 and is grappling with a $22 million deficit.
And the pool of potential pupils is shrinking as the Trump administration works to sharply reduce the number of international students coming to the United States while cutting federal funding for academic and scientific research.
But New York’s college sector continues to grow as its major institutions power through the headwinds and new entrants either establish operations or merge their way into the city.
Employment at private colleges and universities in the city increased about 5% to a record 170,000 in April, according to the state Labor Department, while nationally higher ed jobs declined by 3%. The city’s Economic Development Corp. counted 516,000 college students in 2024, the most recently available numbers.
“There is a flight to quality and students are choosing names they know,” said Ed Venit, who has spent 20 years researching trends in higher education. “Columbia, New York University, Fordham and St. John’s all have brand names. You have Ivy League, Ivy League-adjacent and Fordham with its strong regional identity.”
Vanderbilt illustrates why New York is so attractive to both students and the institutions recruiting them.
Start with the city’s unrivaled attractions. On the first day of classes, the students went to the Upper West Side, SoHo, Little Italy, and Greenwich Village, in part by bus and Citibike. “New York is really their classroom,” Kellerhouse said.
Internships are key for Vanderbilt and no place can offer more opportunities than New York. Vanderbilt’s program requires a 20 to 25-hour-a-week internship and it established more than 140 for the first group of students, including at museums like the Whitney, the High Line, nonprofits like Safe Horizons and several law firms.
MORE: Inside NYC’s K-Shaped Economy: A Few Do Well, Most Do Not
Vanderbilt counts 10,000 alumni working in New York, the highest number anywhere, an increase of almost 2,000 in recent years. The new campus will allow the school to strengthen its ties to that network.
Also crucial are the strong academic reputations of the city’s other colleges and universities.
“Students who are paying for their education are voting with their feet,” said Preston Cooper, an expert on higher education at the American Enterprise Institute. “Lower quality schools have seen a plunge in enrollment. Those with the best education have seen their enrollments grow.”
Admittedly, not all schools in the city are thriving. The New School has seen its enrollment fall to 8,500 in the last academic year from slightly more than 10,000 in 2001 and its finances are shaky.
For other institutions in trouble there are options. With its future in doubt, Marymount Manhattan College on the Upper East Side merged with Northeastern University of Boston, which is trying to build a bigger footprint by taking over small colleges across the country.
“We want to be in New York,” Northeastern President Joseph Aoun said when the deal was announced in 2024. “No institution, even the constellation of institutions that exists in New York, can meet all the needs.”
Increasing the number of private colleges and universities in the city was a priority of the Adams administration, which in 2024 put out a major report which said the sector contributed $35 billion a year to the city’s economy. The new team at City Hall is equally committed to the sector.
“The Mamdani administration will continue building partnerships with our city’s leading research and educational institutions to expand opportunities for working-class New Yorkers and ensure that New York remains a global destination for young talent,” said spokesperson Cassio Mendoza.
Meanwhile, the public City University of New York, with more than 275,000 students, has seen its enrollment grow by 21,000 since 2021.
Federal efforts to restrict international students will be a key factor as the fall semester begins.
The number of international students applying to U.S. schools fell by 10% for the new academic year. Columbia University and NYU may face big challenges. One quarter of NYU students and 18% of Columbia students come from abroad. Columbia did not provide information on its enrollment for the new semester. Columbia did not supply information on international students. NYU did not either, but the school, which last year enrolled 57,000 degree-seeking students and employs slightly more than 28,000 people, knows what is at stake.
“We are a global university, and our international students are part of the fabric of NYU and our international student enrollment remains strong,” said spokesperson Joseph Tirella. 
Vanderbilt’s decision to spend more than $100 million on its lease and renovation suggests the city’s strengths will win out.
“New York is essential to our vision,” the school’s chancellor, Daniel Diermeier, said at the formal opening of the Chelsea campus on Tuesday. “There are few places in the world where so many of the forces shaping our future work, business and finance, technology and media, arts and culture, public policy, global affairs are present.”

candidates.title: Rikers Misses Deadline to Give Detainees Digital Access to Case Evidence
candidates.what_happened:
The city’s Department of Correction has blown past a new deadline to give Rikers Island  detainees a digital platform to review evidence in their cases. The access was mandated by the City Council last year which gave DOC nine months — until July 1 — to find a vendor and implement the evidence review system […] 
 The post  Rikers Misses Deadline to Give Detainees Digital Access to Case Evidence  appeared first on  The City Reporter .

sources.retrieved_text:
The city’s Department of Correction has blown past a new deadline to give Rikers Island detainees a digital platform to review evidence in their cases.
The access was mandated by the City Council last year which gave DOC nine months — until July 1 — to find a vendor and implement the evidence review system through tablets or another secure platform.
The legislation could have a game-changing impact for detainees at the scandal-scarred jail complex who are fighting criminal cases. About 85% of the nearly 6,500 people held on Rikers Island are awaiting trial and have not been convicted of a crime.
There’s no timeline in place to meet the new legal requirement. A jail source told The City Reporter that security concerns had slowed the project.
“It’s been a long time coming, but they just haven’t got it done yet,” said Zachary Katznelson, executive director of the Independent Rikers Commission, which advocates for the closure of the jail complex and wrote a report advocating for digital access.
The DOC has been working on it for at least two years and is in talks with a tech company called Lighting Law which provides similar evidence-access technology to other lockups around the country, according to multiple jail insiders.
In those locations, each detainee receives an individual account that they can use on their department issued tablet and via computers in law libraries. Their defense lawyers can upload the evidence — including large videos — onto the site.
The delayed implementation comes as a court-appointed remediation manager has ordered top jail officials to come up with a series of other reform plans over the next year after more than a decade of failed similar attempts led by Steve Martin, a federal monitor based in Texas.
MORE: ‘Bedlam’ as Rikers Island Can’t Keep Its Doors Locked
As for the evidence initiative, at stake is the ability for Rikers detainees to fully participate in their defense. Currently, Department Correction officials cannot provide detainees with an easy way to review electronic evidence.
“So to watch videotapes, to listen to phone calls, any of that is incredibly difficult, and sometimes virtually impossible,” Katznelson told The City Reporter. “And that means that people can’t prepare properly for their trials.”
Detainees can receive discovery materials by snail mail or review them by using drives accessible on law library computers located in each jail facility. They can also talk about the case with their lawyers by phone, video conference, or during in-person visits.
But they often struggle to get all the information they need to make informed decisions in court, according to criminal defense lawyers and jail reformers.
“Right now, people in custody face enormous barriers to defending themselves,” City Councilmember Jennifer Gutiérrez (D-Brooklyn), the lead sponsor of the bill, said last September as the bill passed in the Council.
“It is much harder, if not impossible, to meaningfully participate in your own defense simply due to a lack of access,” she added. “Technology has transformed nearly every part of our lives, including our courts and justice system, so it must transform in our jails as well.”
Patrick Rocchio, a DOC spokesperson, said the department is “actively working to finalize a contract for the required technology.”
“And we expect to have more to share on this soon,” he added.
Rocchio declined to detail who at the department was leading the negotiations and why it had dragged on so long.
A jail source familiar with the talks said the department has been worried about potential security lapses in which detainees are granted access to materials they’re not cleared to view. One hypothetical example involved a defendant facing child abuse charges receiving a video of the alleged misconduct. Only defense lawyers should have access to those manner of videos; they are not cleared to be shared online via the Lighting Law site.
MORE: Rikers Remediation Manager Unveils Blueprint for Overhauling City Jails
Lighting Law is already in place in approximately 15 other jails throughout the country.
But none are as large as Rikers.
The tech firm was started by Alisa Brodkowitz, an attorney who represents the families of plane crash victims. She got the idea to create an online access system as she struggled to share information with family members in Ethiopia and Kenya with loved ones who died in a crash of the Boeing 737 Max.
The new Council law did not include any penalty for a failure to implement the initiative.
But the ongoing delay could open the department to a potential class action lawsuit by detainees seeking better access to evidence.
The DOC has blown past several other legally mandated deadlines.
The department was obligated to issue a report by May 1 updating the public on its broad plan to close Rikers. The DOC also had recent deadlines for a report detailing ways it plans to reform the department, as well as one explaining how it uses powers to let some people serving a year or less out early.
“These are answers that New Yorkers are hungry for,” Katznelson said. “How are we going to have a system that actually keeps people safe? How are we going to have a system that actually is effective at improving public safety instead of hurting it?”

candidates.title: Chicago Apartment Manager Settles Housing Discrimination Lawsuit
candidates.what_happened: Chicago's Fulton Grace Realty resolved lawsuits over alleged discrimination against voucher holders, committing to retrain its leasing agents.

sources.retrieved_text:
Chicago apartment company Fulton Grace Realty settled a pair of lawsuits that said the company discriminated against housing choice voucher holders.
Hope Fair Housing Center, Northside Community Resources and five voucher holders filed the lawsuits in 2025, seeking damages and changes to the way Fulton Grace treats voucher applicants.
The lawsuit said Fulton Grace discriminated against prospective tenants with housing vouchers who interacted with the company's agents when searching for apartments. It said agents would stop communicating with the prospective tenants, deny their applications or use irrelevant criteria to reject applications once they learned of the housing vouchers.
Hope Fair Housing Center and Northside Community Resources conducted roughly 30 fair housing tests between 2022 and 2024, in which people posing as renters applied for the company's apartments, Block Club Chicago reported. In 20 cases, the groups found evidence of source-of-income discrimination based on voucher use.
Fulton Grace responded to a request for comment with a statement from President and founder TJ Rubin.
“We welcome the opportunity to continue partnering with third parties to ensure our agents maintain compliance with the Fair Housing Act and the Illinois Human Rights Act, including its protections against housing discrimination based on source of income, along with all other applicable local fair housing laws,” Rubin said. “We've worked hard to resolve these disputed claims in a way that's acceptable to everyone involved, and we hold ourselves to the highest standards in doing so. That said, this settlement is a good-faith resolution and does not represent any finding of liability or fault on the part of Fulton Grace.”
Rubin added that the company has always focused on robust training in many aspects of real estate, including fair housing, and that the company is enhancing its training and materials as part of the settlement. He said it is also expanding guidance provided to property owners to further support fair housing practices.
As a result of the settlement, Fulton Grace agreed to pay an undisclosed amount to the plaintiffs and change its application practices.
The company agreed to retrain all of its leasing agents and employees within three months. It has more than 400 leasing agents across Illinois. The company also agreed to designate a liaison to work with internal and external stakeholders to ensure equal opportunity for voucher applicants.
For one year, between August 2026 and August 2027, the company will also waive application fees for applicants using vouchers and other income-based subsidies.
“We hope other leasing agencies, management companies, and other stakeholders take note of the changes Fulton Grace made to its income and credit screening, and ensure their own policies are not blanket barriers to considering qualified Voucher applicants,” MacKenzie Speer, program counsel at Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights, said in a release.

Global investment firm EQT Real Estate has sold off a large Southeast industrial portfolio.
The global investment firm sold a 10M SF logistics portfolio spanning 46 buildings in the Carolinas, Georgia, Florida and Alabama, the company announced Thursday. The buyer was California-based LBA Realty.
The sale was made through the company's EQT Real Estate Industrial Value Fund V. The firm didn't disclose the sale price.
The Class-A industrial portfolio averages 230K SF per building and can accommodate a wide range of uses, from third-party logistics to regional distribution to advanced manufacturing. The buildings sit in 10 Southeast markets, including Charlotte; Savannah, Georgia; Birmingham, Alabama; and Tampa, Florida.
EQT said industrial properties in the region have become more valuable as it has gained population this decade.
All age groups in the South grew faster than in any other region between 2020 and 2025, with the Southeast accounting for many of the fastest-growing counties in the country, according to a June U.S. census report. In those five years, the South experienced a 6% population growth, nearly double the nation's growth at 3.1%
"People and industry continue moving to the Southeast, and logistics demand has followed both," EQT Global Chief Investment Officer Matthew Brodnik said in a statement.
"We identified that theme clearly when we acquired this portfolio, and our local teams did fantastic work adding value through leasing and hands-on management, building by building," he said. "With the region experiencing sustained positive tailwinds, the transaction marks a natural point to crystallize our investment while offering a meaningful runway for its next phase of growth.”
JLL's John Huguenard, Trent Agnew and Will McCormack represented EQT in the deal.
EQT has been active on both the buyer and seller sides of industrial deals over the past year.
Earlier this month, the company sold a 4.4M SF portfolio consisting of 20 industrial assets in the Midwest to Houston-based SparrowHawk for just under $440M. In November, it sold an 8.7M SF industrial portfolio spanning 13 markets for an undisclosed price.
EQT also purchased an industrial portfolio this month from Rexford Industrial Realty for $1.2B. And in May, the firm announced it would partner with cold storage company Americold Realty Trust and invest $1.1B into a 12-building, 124M SF cold storage portfolio.
EQT has $58B in assets under management, owning and operating more than 2,000 properties spanning 450M SF.

Accounts associated with President Donald Trump traded shares in around 30 real estate firms among more than 1,000 June transactions.
Trump made 1,056 trades between June 1 and June 24, including at least 46 moves involving real estate firms and still more involving investment giants like Blackstone and Apollo Global Management. The president, who also invested in eight fixed-income multifamily securities around the country, was a net seller of real estate shares over the month, according to a new ethics disclosure from the White House.
The president’s biggest moves of the month in the space were the sales of shares worth between $100K and $250K each of CoStar Group, SBA Communications and Vici Properties on June 18. He made seven other sales of those stocks over the reporting period and purchased between $1K and $15K in CoStar shares on June 3.
The president made at least 17 purchases of real estate-related stock while simultaneously making 29 sales across the reporting period, according to a Bisnow analysis.
The financial disclosures provide a range for the dollar value of the transaction, not an exact amount or share count, but the midpoint of purchases against sales suggest the president lightened his commercial real estate exposure by around $350K over the month.
Trump’s accounts are managed by The Trump Organization, which says it makes the transactions without any input from the president or his family.
“The President's investment holdings are maintained exclusively in fully discretionary accounts managed by independent third-party financial institutions,” a Trump Organization spokesperson told Yahoo Finance. “Those institutions, not the President, have sole and exclusive authority over all investment decisions.”
Real estate trades accounted for 5.2% of the president’s trades during the reporting period. Across all transactions, Trump made 495 stock purchases and 561 sales.
Trump made six trades in the second-largest band of transactions, ranging from $50K to $100K, selling Airbnb and CoStar and buying American Tower Corp., PennyMac Mortgage Investment Trust, Prologis and Zillow.
He made 13 real estate trades between $15K and $50K, and the remaining 24 were no more than $15K.
Trump made two purchases of CoreWeave stock over the reporting period and also purchased shares in Ares Management, Everus Construction Group, Ryman Hospitality, Terreno Realty and Rocket Cos., among others.
Other notable sales included stock in CBRE, Crown Castle, Simon Property Group, Realty Income Corp., Lennar and AvalonBay Communities.
The president’s bond purchases range from $15K to $50K for student housing at Texas A&M University up to a $500K to $1M note for the Louisiana Housing Corp.
The latest ethics disclosure comes nearly two months after the White House revealed that Trump made some $2.2B during his first year back in office, quadrupling his revenue from 2024. The majority of those earnings came from his cryptocurrency business, which includes a stablecoin venture called World Liberty Financial and a meme token.

sources.retrieved_text:
Cold storage is undergoing a market shift, posting negative net absorption in the first half of 2026 and reaching a new record high for vacancy.
Nationwide, cold storage facilities recorded net negative absorption of 56 million cubic feet, according to a new report from Newmark. It is the first time absorption has fallen into negative territory for the property type since 2007.
In addition, 41 million cubic feet of new supply came online, helping push the overall vacancy rate to 7.7%, up from a 20-year record high at the end of 2025.
Demand for cold storage has been impacted by a pullback in grocery shopping by consumers, pinched by increasing food costs.
Food prices are up more than 30% compared to 2019, according to the report. That, along with a cut in SNAP benefits and high gas prices, has contributed to a 1.8% year-over-year drop in grocery unit sales.
"Relatively static real spending has led to leaner, more precisely managed inventories across the supply chain, contributing to today’s softer cold storage demand environment," according to the report's authors, Newmark’s Amy Binstein, Lisa DeNight, Jamil Harkness and David Bitner.
As in other sectors, the pain is coming unevenly. Cold storage warehouses built since 2020 have fielded almost all the new demand, and older facilities have borne the brunt of the vacancy.
Warehouses built before 2006 account for 68% of all vacant cold storage space and carry an 8.2% vacancy rate, while those built between 2006 and 2019 are 3.4% vacant.
Nearly all the space that was backfilled in the first half of this year was built in 2020 or later, and almost all the negative net absorption was in warehouses built in 2006 or earlier.
A disconnect persists between the spaces that users are looking for and the ones under construction now. The average cold storage lease signed in the last five years was 125K SF, while the average size of under-construction projects is 300K SF, which may account for longer lease-up periods for some projects coming online, the report's authors said.
But those new projects are expensive to build relative to their traditional industrial counterparts. Cold storage warehouses cost $130 to $350 per SF to build, compared to $80 to $150 per SF for regular warehouses, according to Newmark. Two of the top five markets for cold storage by square footage, New York-Philadelphia and Los Angeles-Inland Empire, have nearly no new cold storage under construction, and the buildings average 29 to 52 years old.
Cold storage warehouse users represent nearly 36% of buyers, up from 32% in 2025 and just 10% in 2024. One of those transactions was Walmart's $223M purchase of a 2010-built Riverside, California, cold storage warehouse. The trend gives fuel to the fear that these users will have less need to lease speculative space.

If you need a new refrigerator condenser or thermostat, Parts Town Unlimited will have you covered from Pendergrass, Georgia.
The parts supplier focused on food service, appliances and HVAC original equipment manufacturer parts has leased 538,400 SF at Building 1 of Jackson 85 North Business Park, some 100 miles north of Downtown Atlanta, according to a press release.
Jackson 85 North will serve as Parts Town’s largest global fulfillment center behind its facilities in Chicago, Phoenix and Munich and will support more than 140 local jobs, according to the release. The new facility can deliver parts to more than 90% of the U.S. within two days.
“By placing greater depth and breadth of mission-critical OEM parts closer to customers across the Southeast, we can reduce transit times and costs,” Parts Town CEO Bill Geary said in the release.
The lease covers the entire building, which is owned and developed by Trammell Crow Co. and CBRE Investment Management. Wilson Hull Neal’s Bilijack Bell, Joseph Rogers, Conner Dickinson and Will Geraghty represented the landlords, while SK Commercial Realty brokered for the tenant.
Jackson 85 North still has a second 1M SF speculative Class-A warehouse on its 215 acres as part of the first phase of its development, according to the release.
LEASES
Gym chain EōS Fitness inked a long-term 38K SF lease for a new location at 965 North Point Drive in Alpharetta, part of the North Point Commons shopping center. The gym is taking over a space previously occupied by the defunct arts and crafts retailer Joann Fabric and Crafts.
Joann shuttered all its Georgia locations under bankruptcy last year.
The landlord, Realty Income, represented itself, while SRS Real Estate Partners represented the tenant.
ASSIGNMENTS
Evergreen Medical Properties has tapped Transwestern’s John Lopez and Bo Stuart to lease up Northside Alpharetta Medical Campus, a four-building, 415K SF medical office property at 3400 Old Milton Parkway in North Fulton County. More than 200 medical tenants within the Northside Hospital network are tenants in the property.
***
Selig Enterprises Inc. has tapped Partners Real Estate’s John Zintak, Will Porter and Gracie Swan to lease the remaining 30K SF of space available at the firm’s 1105 West Peachtree, a 675K SF trophy office tower in Midtown that is home to Google and law firm Smith Gambrell & Russell.
The tower is part of a larger mixed-use project that includes luxury condominium tower 40 West 12th and the Epicurean Atlanta hotel.
Beyond the office building, the trio is also helping Selig lure potential tenants that could kick off new developments at the firm’s Midtown land holdings, including 1125 Peachtree St., 48 12th St. and 1200 Spring St., the Atlanta Business Chronicle reported.
DEVELOPMENT
Thompson Thrift has broken ground on Avira at Silver Comet Trail, a 319-unit apartment complex in Powder Springs that is expected to deliver by October of next year. Located at the corner of Georgia Highway 278 and Isley Stamper Road, the site is adjacent to the more than 60-mile Silver Comet pedestrian trail, which runs from Smyrna to the border of Alabama.
Amenities will include a resort-style swimming pool, fitness center, pickleball court, dog park and pet spa, as well as coworking suites, grilling areas and other lifestyle-focused amenities, according to a release. Thompson Thrift capitalized the project with equity from its Thompson Thrift 2026 Multifamily Development fund.
***
The world’s largest retailer, Walmart, plans to develop a high-tech fulfillment center in Carnesville, creating 1,000 new jobs and investing $1.3B in the Franklin County community, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp announced this week.
Walmart plans to develop a 1.5M SF automated facility at the Franklin 85 Logistics Center, designed to help the retailer fulfill same-day and next-day shipping across the U.S.
The Georgia Department of Economic Development's Elizabeth McLean represented the state in incentive negotiations with Walmart.
SALES
Dallas-based S2 Capital sold The Bowie, a 350-unit, garden-style apartment complex at 8800 Dunwoody Place in Sandy Springs, to an undisclosed buyer for an undisclosed price, according to a Newmark press release.
The nearly 30-acre property in Central Perimeter is 86% leased. Newmark’s Brooks Colquitt, James Wilber, David Gutting, Derrick Bloom and Hunter Amos brokered the sale. Fulton County property records did not reflect a sale as of press time.
S2 purchased the complex in 2022 for $68M, according to Fulton County property records. The firm obtained a $54.5M loan from Acore Capital at the time, which was set to mature in December 2027.
Fulton County valued the property at $27.6M earlier this year, a nearly 60% discount to S2’s purchase price.
Sherman Residential purchased Celadon on Club, a 352-unit apartment complex in Lawrenceville, from an LLC attached to Atlanta-based Oxford Properties for an undisclosed sum. The Class-A, garden-style apartments off Club Drive were developed in 2023.
Gwinnett County did not reflect a current sales transaction, but the county valued the property at $55M earlier this year.
***
Minnesota-based The Terrace Group paid $12.65M for Columbia Colony Senior Residences, a 62-year-old apartment community at 2999 Continental Road in Atlanta, from Utah-based Columbia Colony Whitaker LLC, according to sales tax records in the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority database.
According to Fulton County property records, the LLC is tied to Peak Capital Partners, which paid $9.2M in 2019 for the 120-unit property.
***
1325 Virginia Hospitality LLC purchased the Sonesta Atlanta Airport North, a 378-room hotel off Virginia Avenue near Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, from an LLC tied to Tremont Realty Capital in Massachusetts, according to sales tax records in the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority database.
The local LLC, which is tied to the Lawrenceville law firm Mills Walls Alioto, is connected to a $10M project that recently underwent a room refresh, according to JLL, which previously marketed the property for sale, according to an internet archive of the website.

The Federal Housing Administration (FHA) is expected to go live in January with VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T, alongside the existing Classic FICO product, as part of a broad credit score modernization effort, according to industry sources who spoke with HousingWire.
In a call with lenders earlier this week, FHA representatives told participants they will be able to deliver any of the three models for case files dated on or after Jan. 2027, sources said. The shift follows the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD’s April announcement that FHA would adopt FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 for FHA loans.
Based on the current discussions, lenders expect model consistency will be required at the loan level, meaning they would not be allowed to mix VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T (or other combinations) across co-borrowers on the same file.
HUD and FHA did not immediately respond to HousingWire‘s request for comment.
“You have to have model consistency with your borrowers in the same application, which I think makes some sense. It limits the gaming there,” a person familiar with the discussions said.
At the same time, FHA has said in conversations with industry participants that Classic FICO will not be sunset as part of the rollout, sources added.
Mortgage executives say keeping Classic FICO in production aligns with conditions in the secondary market, where many mortgage-backed securities (MBS) are still collateralized and traded based on Classic FICO. An abrupt retirement of the legacy model could affect “bond liquidity,” one executive said.
Unlike the conventional market overseen by the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), the FHA rollout is expected to apply to all lenders at launch, according to the sources. FHFA’s own move toward FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 has followed a more staggered approach with large lenders actively engaged in testing and implementation.
For FHA, the pricing impact of the model change is expected to be more limited.
FHA generally does not vary base pricing for individual borrowers using credit score and loan-to-value matrices in the same way that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac do with loan-level price adjustments (LLPAs). Instead, FHA’s economics are driven primarily through its upfront and annual mortgage insurance premiums (MIPs).

sources.retrieved_text:
Today, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh gave his much-anticipated Jackson Hole speech, which I previewed in today’s episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler. My primary take from the speech is that Warsh will vote for a rate hike if inflation data doesn’t improve and labor data is stable.
My main concern with Warsh is that at some point the Fed will have enough votes to hike rates, and if he doesn’t go along with them, markets will always see him as a Trump puppet. At that point, markets will look to Beth Hammack as the Fed Chair, which wouldn’t be good for the relationship between the Fed and the markets. For now, after this speech, I believe Warsh will vote for a rate hike if there are enough votes.
What matters now?
The market has already priced in rate hikes on the long end, so not much is happening right now; currently, the 10-year yield is at 4.72%. So the question is: where do we go from here? I want us to focus less on Kevin Warsh and the Fed and more on what actually matters for rates.
1. The Iran conflict has to come to an end or at least not get worse
The Fed hawks have made the Iran conflict a very big talking point of being hawkish, and it’s still going on, so if you want lower rates and better inflation data, the conflict has to end or at least not get worse, with oil prices below $82. I believe the fear of the conflict escalating has the hawks nervous and oil and diesel prices need to come down to alleviate that.
In fact, President Trump’s own economic talking point before the conflict was that if oil prices fall, everything will go down with them. I believe a range of $67-$82 will work; we are currently a tad above that, but just the threat of more escalation and no deal will always make the Fed more hawkish.
2. The trade war can’t get worse
The Fed recently wrote a paper on tariffs and their impact on the economy where they analyzed 125,000 US households’ transactions to measure how the 2025 tariffs affected spending. “Tariffs passed through 15-20% to retail prices, raising affected-good prices 1-2% but households cut spending by 4%, 3 to 4 times the price increase.”
The Federal Reserve was going to let trade-war inflation pass through the economy this year and still provide two to three rate cuts as the year started. This was also because labor data was softening toward the end of last year. However, inflation data worsened before the iran conflict, which forced the hawks to get more hawkish. I am sure that the Fed hawks are not thrilled that we started another trade war with Canada, one of our biggest trading partners .
In any case, inflation needs to improve, and the trade war getting worse isn’t going to get the Fed hawks to stand pat. The Fed really wants PCE inflation to head back toward 2%, and it’s not there yet. The PCE inflation data doesn’t have the big shelter disinflation factor, so it will be harder to get this back down without Trump working toward that progress.
3. Labor data still matters
Fed hawks and the Fed in general have said they don’t mind low job growth because the labor force isn’t growing. The bond market has taken notice and traded yields properly on this premise. The unemployment rate is 4.1%, and jobless claims data is historically very low. If anything changes with this premise, some of the Fed members will not vote for a rate hike, and therefore the worst in pricing and rates is already here. You can have some room to go lower in yields if labor softens up.
Conclusion
I am not a fan of Kevin Warsh as Fed chair, but today I did get the sense that he understands the concerns of the hawks, and at least if there was a unanimous vote to raise rates, he would join the vote. However, we need to move past Warsh and focus on what matters; two of the three concerns above are things in the Trump administration’s control, and one isn’t, so they have a lot of work to do to get rates lower.

Michael Haack has joined the board of Champion Homes Inc. as an independent director, the company announced, bringing the manufactured housing builder’s board to seven members, six of whom are independent. Haack’s appointment was effective Aug. 24, 2026. He will serve on the board’s compensation committee, according to the company announcement. Haack currently serves as president and CEO of Dallas-based Eagle Materials Inc., where he is also a director. Eagle Materials is a U.S. manufacturer of heavy construction products and light building materials, including Portland cement and gypsum wallboard used in residential, commercial and infrastructure projects nationwide. During his tenure at Eagle, Haack has led more than $1.6 billion in acquisitions, the company said. That M&A background and exposure to core building materials markets offer additional insight for a manufactured housing company navigating input costs, supply chain volatility and capital allocation decisions. “Michael brings deep experience leading complex industrial organizations – a perspective that inevitably will be beneficial to our board,” Michael Berman, chair of the Champion Homes board of directors, said in the announcement. Before joining Eagle Materials, Haack spent more than 17 years at Halliburton in senior manufacturing, operational and global leadership roles. His positions there included work across manufacturing, supply chain, quality, reliability, regional operations and global strategy. As global operations manager for Sperry Drilling, he led more than 8,000 employees across major oil and gas markets.

Haack said he sees Champion Homes as operating at the intersection of manufacturing and innovation while addressing an important segment of housing demand. “I am honored to join the Champion Homes board and look forward to working with my fellow directors and the management team,” Haack said. “Champion Homes operates at the intersection of manufacturing and innovation and serves an important housing need.” Haack has served as Eagle’s president and CEO since 2019, helping guide the company through a strategic and operational overhaul, including technology investments and a shift from a decentralized plant structure to a more integrated network. Champion Homes, which relies on a multi-plant manufacturing footprint to produce HUD-code manufactured homes and modular units, has been focused on plant efficiency, throughput and margins amid ongoing affordability challenges. Haack also serves on the board of Terra CO2 and has previously served on the board of 2Source Manufacturing Inc. He is additionally involved with advisory organizations connected to MIT and Texas A&M University. He holds an MBA from Rice University, a master’s degree in industrial engineering from Texas A&M University and a bachelor’s degree in industrial engineering from Purdue University.

- Fluor is nearing construction completion on Novelis’ $5 billion aluminum recycling plant in Bay Minette, Alabama, the company confirmed in a statement to Construction Dive.
- The Irving, Texas-based contractor recently laid off 66 employees on the site, effective July 31, according to Alabama’s Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification database. Companies generally must file WARN notices for layoffs of 50 or more workers at a single site.

Fluor, which is providing engineering, procurement and construction management services on the project, made major strides during construction last year. In the second quarter of 2025, for example, crews installed the plant’s hot mill housings during foundation and excavation work. About 1,000 workers were working on site at the time, according to Novelis.
Portions of the facility have since moved into commissioning, according to the Novelis’ fourth quarter and full fiscal year 2026 report. Novelis reported it began commissioning the cold mill in Bay Minette in March.

NYC expands free rooftop tours at historic Manhattan Municipal Building
Credit: Ed Reed/Mayoral Photography Office on Flickr
Larger groups are now permitted to attend the city’s free tours of the historic David N. Dinkins Manhattan Municipal Building following growing demand. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS) Commissioner Yume Kitasei on Friday announced expanded access to “Centre 360,” a panoramic experience inside the Beaux-Arts government building’s 36th-floor cupola, increasing the maximum group size from five to eight. The move comes just months after the tours launched in June following a $6 million renovation, with reservations for the experience selling out in less than two minutes.
Designed by William K. Kendall of McKim, Mead & White, the firm behind the original Penn Station and Brooklyn Museum, the Municipal Building was constructed to serve the growing city following the consolidation of the five boroughs in 1898, as 6sqft previously reported.
Influenced by the City Beautiful movement’s call for grand civic buildings, the structure features a towering classical exterior with Roman-inspired details, including a central arch modeled after the Arch of Constantine.
The first building in New York to incorporate a subway station at its base, the Municipal Building was designated an individual landmark by the city’s Landmarks Preservation Commission in 1966. The station entrance was modeled after the arched entrance of the Palazzo Farnese in Rome and features vaulted Guastavino tiles.
Perched atop the building is the “Civic Fame” statue, a gilded copper figure designed by Adolph A. Weinman. The 25-foot-tall statue carries a shield bearing the city’s coat of arms, a branch of leaves, and a mural crown with five points symbolizing each borough.
The building was renamed the David N. Dinkins Manhattan Municipal Building in 2015 in honor of the former mayor.
Mamdani first announced in February that the rooftop would open to the public following a $6 million restoration that repaired the cupola, installed glass safety barriers, and restored the rotunda landing. Though intended to be accessible to the public when the building first opened, the cupola had been off-limits for nearly 100 years.
Launched in June, the tour allows visitors to walk a full circle around the cupola for 360-degree views of the city from nearly 600 feet above the ground, with many famous landmarks visible in the distance. Reservations initially allowed groups of up to five people.
According to the city, the tours have been immensely popular, with reservations selling out within two minutes each month after they open. Groups of up to eight visitors will now be permitted, allowing as many as 2,000 people to visit the cupola each month.
To further expand access, DCAS will also offer first-come, first-served walk-in spots when last-minute cancellations or no-shows create availability.
“Since we opened the cupola this summer, New Yorkers have shown us just how much they want to experience this iconic landmark,” Mamdani said. “When demand is this strong, our job is to find a way to open the doors wider.”
“Today we’re doing just that by expanding reservation groups from five to eight and adding walk-in access when space becomes available, so hundreds more people can take in these incredible views each month,” he added.
DCAS offers eight tours Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Each session has two reservations available, with groups of up to four people permitted per reservation. Children under 18 must be accompanied by an adult and be at least 42 inches tall.
Visitors must reserve tickets through the online reservation system and present a valid photo ID upon arrival. Reservations open on the first day of each month. Learn more about the experience and make a reservation here.
